0.20.0 [2021-04-19]¶
- Support display of animated images kitty +kitten icat animation.gif. See
Animation for details on animation support in the kitty
graphics protocol.
- A new keyboard reporting protocol with various advanced features that can be used by full screen terminal programs and even games, see Comprehensive keyboard handling in terminals (#3248)
- Backward incompatibility: Session files now use the full launch
command with all its capabilities. However, the syntax of the command is
slightly different from before. In particular watchers are now specified
directly on launch and environment variables are set using --env.
- Allow setting colors when creating windows using the launch command.
- A new option tab_powerline_style to control the appearance of the tab
bar when using the powerline tab bar style.
- A new option scrollback_fill_enlarged_window to fill extra lines in
the window when the window is expanded with lines from the scrollback
(#3371)
- diff kitten: Implement recursive diff over SSH (#3268)
- ssh kitten: Allow using python instead of the shell on the server, useful if the shell used is a non-POSIX compliant one, such as fish (#3277)
- Add support for the color settings stack that XTerm copied from us without acknowledgement and decided to use incompatible escape codes for.
- Add entries to the terminfo file for some user capabilities that are shared with XTerm (#3193)
- The launch command now does more sophisticated resolving of executables to run. The system-wide PATH is used first, then system specific default paths, and finally the PATH inside the shell.
- Double clicking on empty tab bar area now opens a new tab (#3201)
- kitty @ ls: Show only environment variables that are different for each window, by default.
- When passing a directory or a non-executable file as the program to run to kitty opens it with the shell or by parsing the shebang, instead of just failing.
- Linux: Fix rendering of emoji followed by the graphics variation selector not being colored with some fonts (#3211)
- Unicode input: Fix using index in select by name mode not working for indices larger than 16. Also using an index does not filter the list of matches. (#3219)
- Wayland: Add support for the text input protocol (#3410)
- Wayland: Fix mouse handling when using client side decorations
- Wayland: Fix un-maximizing a window not restoring its size to what it was before being maximized
- GNOME/Wayland: Improve window decorations the titlebar now shows the window title. Allow running under Wayland on GNOME by default. (#3284)
- Panel kitten: Allow setting WM_CLASS (#3233)
- macOS: Add menu items to close the OS window and the current tab (#3240, #3246)
- macOS: Allow opening script and command files with kitty (#3366)
- Also detect gemini:// URLs when hovering with the mouse (#3370)
- When using a non-US keyboard layout and pressing ctrl+key when the key matches an English key, send that to the program running in the terminal automatically (#2000)
- When matching shortcuts, also match on shifted keys, so a shortcut defined as ctrl+plus will match a keyboard where you have to press shift+equal to get the plus key (#2000)
- Fix extra space at bottom of OS window when using the fat layout with the tab bar at the top (#3258)
- Fix window icon not working on X11 with 64bits (#3260)
- Fix OS window sizes under 100px resulting in scaled display (#3307)
- Fix rendering of ligatures in the latest release of Cascadia code, which for some reason puts empty glyphs after the ligature glyph rather than before it (#3313)
- Improve handling of infinite length ligatures in newer versions of FiraCode and CascadiaCode. Now such ligatures are detected based on glyph naming convention. This removes the gap in the ligatures at cell boundaries (#2695)

- Fix inactive tab closing causing active tab to change (#3398)

- Add support for hyperlinks from terminal programs.
Controlled via allow_hyperlinks (#68)

- A new Hyperlinked grep kitten to easily search files and open the results at the matched line by clicking on them.

- Allow specifying watchers in session files and via a command line argument (#2933)

if one of the windows has some activity after it was last focused
(#2515)
- macOS: Switch to using the User Notifications framework for notifications. The current notifications framework has been deprecated in Big Sur. The new framework only allows notifications from signed and notarized applications, so people using kitty from homebrew/source are out of luck. Complain to Apple.
- When in the main screen and a program grabs the mouse, do not use the scroll wheel events to scroll the scrollback buffer, instead send them to the program (#2939)

- Fix a regression that broke kitten_alias (#2952)
- Fix a regression that broke the move_window_to_top action (#2953)
- Fix a memory leak when changing font sizes
- Fix some lines in the scrollback buffer not being properly rendered after a window resize/font size change (#2619)

that separate the inactive window from a neighbor. Note that setting
a non-zero window margin overrides this and causes all borders to be drawn.
The old behavior of drawing all borders can be restored via the
draw_minimal_borders setting in kitty.conf. (#699)
- macOS: Add an option macos_window_resizable to control if kitty
top-level windows are resizable using the mouse or not (#698)
- macOS: Use a custom mouse cursor that shows up well on both light and dark backgrounds (#359)

- Fix triple-click to select line not working when the entire line is filled (#703)
- When dragging to select with the mouse “grab” the mouse so that if it strays into neighboring windows, the selection is still updated (#624)
- When clicking in the margin/border area of a window, map the click to the nearest cell in the window. Avoids selection with the mouse failing when starting the selection just outside the window.
- When drag-scrolling stop the scroll when the mouse button is released.
- Fix a regression in the previous release that caused pasting large amounts of text to be duplicated (#709)

- Show a bell symbol on the tab if a bell occurs in one of the windows in the tab and the window is not the currently focused window

- When triple-clicking select all wrapped lines belonging to a single logical line.

- macOS: When the macos_titlebar_color is set to background change the titlebar colors to match the current background color of the active kitty window

- Don’t fail to start if the user deletes the hintstyle key from their fontconfig configuration.

- Fix passing @text to other programs such as when viewing the scrollback buffer not working correctly if kitty is itself scrolled up.

- Fix tab title not changing to reflect the window title when switching between different windows in a tab
- Ignore -e if it is specified on the command line. This is for compatibility with broken software that assumes terminals should run with an -e option to execute commands instead of just passing the commands as arguments.
0.9.0 [2018-04-15]¶
- A new kitty command shell to allow controlling kitty via commands. Press ctrl+shift+escape to run the shell.
- The hints kitten has become much more powerful. Now in addition to URLs you can use it to select word, paths, filenames, lines, etc. from the screen. These can be inserted into the terminal, copied to clipboard or sent to external programs.
- Linux: Switch to libxkbcommon for keyboard handling. It allows kitty to support XCompose and dead keys and also react to keyboard remapping/layout change without needing a restart.
- Add support for multiple-key-sequence shortcuts
- A new remote control command set-colors to change the current and/or configured colors.
- When double-clicking to select a word, select words that continue onto the next/prev line as well.
- Add an include directive for the config files to read multiple config files
- Improve mouse selection for windows with padding. Moving the mouse into the padding area now acts as if the mouse is over the nearest cell.
- Allow setting all 256 terminal colors in the config file
- Fix using kitty --single-instance to open a new window in a running kitty instance, not respecting the --directory flag
- URL hints: Exclude trailing punctuation from URLs
- URL hints: Launch the browser from the kitty parent process rather than the hints kitten. Fixes launching on some systems where xdg-open doesn’t like being run from a kitten.
- Allow using rectangle select mode by pressing shift in addition to the rectangle select modifiers even when the terminal program has grabbed the mouse.

0.8.0 [2018-02-24]¶
- A framework for kittens, that is, small terminal programs designed to run inside kitty and extend its capabilities. Examples include unicode input and selecting URLs with the keyboard.
- Input arbitrary unicode characters by pressing Ctrl+Shift+u. You can choose characters by name, by hex code, by recently used, etc. There is even and editable Favorites list.
- Open URLs using only the keyboard. kitty has a new “hints mode”. Press Ctrl+Shift+e and all detected URLs on the screen are highlighted with a key to press to open them. The facility is customizable so you can change what is detected as a URL and which program is used to open it.
- Add an option to change the titlebar color of kitty windows on macOS
- Only consider Emoji characters with default Emoji presentation to be two cells wide. This matches the standard. Also add support for the Unicode Emoji variation presentation selector.
- Prevent video tearing during high speed scrolling by syncing draws
to the monitor’s refresh rate. There is a new configuration option to
control this sync_to_monitor.
- When displaying only a single window, use the default background color of the window (which can be changed via escape codes) as the color for the margin and padding of the window.
- Add some non standard terminfo capabilities used by neovim and tmux.
- Fix large drop in performance when using multiple top-level windows on macOS
- Fix save/restore of window sizes not working correctly.
- Remove option to use system wcwidth(). Now always use a wcwidth() based on the Unicode standard. Only sane way.
- Fix a regression that caused a few ligature glyphs to not render correctly in rare circumstances.
- Browsing the scrollback buffer now happens in an overlay window instead of a new window/tab.

0.6.0 [2017-12-18]¶
- Support background transparency via the background_opacity option. Provided that your OS/window manager supports transparency, you can now have kitty render pixels that have only the default background color as semi-transparent.
- Support multiple top level (OS) windows. These windows all share the sprite texture cache on the GPU, further reducing overall resource usage. Use the shortcut ctrl+shift+n to open a new top-level window.
- Add support for a daemon mode using the --single-instance command line option. With this option you can have only a single kitty instance running. All future invocations simply open new top-level windows in the existing instance.
- Support colored emoji
- Use CoreText instead of FreeType to render text on macOS
- Support running on the “low power” GPU on dual GPU macOS machines
- Add a new “grid” window layout
- Drop the dependency on glfw (kitty now uses a modified, bundled copy of glfw)
- Add an option to control the audio bell volume on X11 systems
- Add a command line switch to set the name part of the WM_CLASS window property independently.
- Add a command line switch to set the window title.
- Add more options to customize the tab-bar’s appearance (font styles and separator)
- Allow drag and drop of files into kitty. On drop kitty will paste the file path to the running program.
- Add an option to control the underline style for URL highlighting on hover
- X11: Set the WINDOWID environment variable
- Fix middle and right buttons swapped when sending mouse events to child processes
- Allow selecting in a rectangle by holding down Ctrl+Alt while dragging with the mouse.

- Add an option to control the thickness of lines in box drawing characters
- Increase max. allowed ligature length to nine characters
- Fix text not vertically centered when adjusting line height
- Fix unicode block characters not being rendered properly
- Fix shift+up/down not generating correct escape codes
- Image display: Fix displaying images taller than two screen heights not scrolling properly
0.5.0 [2017-11-19]¶
- Add support for ligature fonts such as Fira Code, Hasklig, etc. kitty now uses harfbuzz for text shaping which allow it to support advanced OpenType features such as contextual alternates/ligatures/combining glyphs/etc.
- Make it easy to select fonts by allowing listing of monospace fonts using: kitty list-fonts
- Add an option to have window focus follow mouse
- Add a keyboard shortcut (ctrl+shift+f11) to toggle fullscreen mode
- macOS: Fix handling of option key. It now behaves just like the alt key on Linux. There is an option to make it type unicode characters instead.
- Linux: Add support for startup notification on X11 desktops. kitty will now inform the window manager when its startup is complete.
- Fix shell prompt being duplicated when window is resized
- Fix crash when displaying more than 64 images in the same session
- Add support for colons in SGR color codes. These are generated by some applications such as neovim when they mistakenly identify kitty as a libvte based terminal.
- Fix mouse interaction not working in apps using obsolete mouse interaction protocols
- Linux: no longer require glew as a dependency
0.4.2 [2017-10-23]¶
- Fix a regression in 0.4.0 that broke custom key mappings
- Fix a regression in 0.4.0 that broke support for non-QWERTY keyboard layouts
- Avoid using threads to reap zombie child processes. Also prevent kitty from hanging if the open program hangs when clicking on a URL.
0.4.0 [2017-10-22]¶
- Support for drawing arbitrary raster graphics (images) in the terminal via a new graphics protocol. kitty can draw images with full 32-bit color using both ssh connections and files/shared memory (when available) for better performance. The drawing primitives support alpha blending and z-index. Images can be drawn both above and below text. See Terminal graphics protocol. for details.
- Refactor kitty’s internals to make it even faster and more efficient. The CPU
usage of kitty + X server while doing intensive tasks such as scrolling a
file continuously in less has been reduced by 50%. There are now two
configuration options repaint_delay and input_delay you can use to
fine tune kitty’s performance vs CPU usage profile. The CPU usage of kitty +
X when scrolling in less is now significantly better than most (all?) other
terminals. See Performance.
- Hovering over URLs with the mouse now underlines them to indicate they can be clicked. Hold down Ctrl+Shift while clicking to open the URL.
- Selection using the mouse is now more intelligent. It does not add blank cells (i.e. cells that have no content) after the end of text in a line to the selection.
- The block cursor in now fully opaque but renders the character under it in the background color, for enhanced visibility.
- Allow combining multiple independent actions into a single shortcut
- Add a new shortcut to pass the current selection to an external program
- Allow creating shortcuts to open new windows running arbitrary commands. You can also pass the current selection to the command as an arguments and the contents of the screen + scrollback buffer as stdin to the command.

Nvidia RTX Spark encrypted firmware slows inference speed to 35% on Linux
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
08:46:29 UTC
17:46:29 KST

Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works
A hands-on look at dual-booting Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop, the GPU clock throttling bug found, and why WSL still wins.
Can you run Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop?
Yes, but it comes with a serious catch. Linux installs and runs on RTX Spark laptops like the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus, including GPU acceleration through Nvidia’s open kernel driver. The problem is clock speed: once the laptop is plugged into wall power, the GPU gets locked to roughly 780 MHz on Linux instead of the 2 GHz-plus it hits on Windows. That turns a chip capable of around 65 tokens per second on a 120 billion parameter model into one struggling to break 14 tokens per second, for reasons tied to power management firmware that Linux currently can’t read.
TL;DR
- Dual-booting Linux works on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop, with a full desktop, GPU acceleration via Nvidia’s open driver, 4K output at 120Hz, and working audio, keyboard, and touchpad once configured correctly.
- A hidden Windows-only component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework manages power delivery between CPU and GPU, and it has no Linux equivalent, which is the root cause of the slowdown.
- GPU clock speed collapses to about 780 MHz on Linux when plugged in, compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows, because the firmware’s power table is encrypted and only the Windows driver can decrypt it.
- Benchmarks on GPT-OSS-120B show the gap clearly: Windows hit 65.4 tokens per second, WSL hit 65.1, the Nvidia DGX Spark hit 61, and native Linux on the same laptop managed only 13.9.
- Memory allocation is a separate headache, since the laptop reserves 96GB of unified memory for the GPU by default and only Windows exposes a setting to change that split, which is required before Linux can see more than a sliver of RAM.
- WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) is the practical middle ground today, since it rides on the Windows driver stack and keeps full GPU boost whether the laptop is plugged in or on battery, while still running Linux-first AI tools like vLLM.
- A real fix depends on Nvidia, specifically on porting the platform controller’s power management logic into its Linux driver, which would effectively turn the laptop into a portable version of the DGX Spark.
Remy.
What makes the RTX Spark laptop different from a normal Windows PC?
The RTX Spark platform, which ships in machines like the MSI Prestige, the Asus ProArt, and the Dell XPS, uses the same GPU design as Nvidia’s DGX Spark desktop unit. But where the DGX Spark ships with Nvidia’s own Linux build out of the box, every one of these laptop variants ships with Windows on ARM.
That distinction matters because Windows on ARM with CUDA support is new. ARM-based Windows machines have existed for a few years, but pairing that architecture with Nvidia’s CUDA stack only became possible with this chip. The laptops also support unified memory configurations up to 128GB, shared between CPU and GPU, which is unusual for a laptop and central to why they’re being marketed at AI developers in the first place.
Because so much of the AI tooling ecosystem, including vLLM and SGLang, is built Linux-first, developers who buy these machines naturally want to know whether they can ditch Windows, or at least dual-boot, without losing performance.
How do you actually install Linux on it?
The process is not plug-and-play. A first attempt using Omarchy (a Linux distribution with Arch roots) failed because, while it already supported the chip on Asus and Dell hardware, the MSI Prestige behaved differently, producing a flickering, unstable display during boot.
Switching to Debian worked more reliably, but still needed workarounds. The installer couldn’t connect to Wi-Fi, so installation required a USB Ethernet adapter. Out of the box, Debian also didn’t recognize the keyboard, touchpad, or GPU, because none of the laptop-specific hardware support was present in a vanilla kernel.
Going back to Omarchy solved the driver problem, since its kernel already bundled Nvidia’s open-source driver. At that point Linux booted properly, but could only see 28GB of the laptop’s 128GB of unified memory. That’s because the laptop’s firmware reserves 96GB for GPU use, and that split is only adjustable from Windows. Dropping the Windows-side GPU memory reservation down to 4GB freed up 120GB for Linux to see once booted. After that adjustment, the laptop ran a full desktop at 4K and 120Hz, with working audio, touchpad, keyboard, and CUDA acceleration.
Getting video output over HDMI during the install process was its own obstacle. Early in the process, the laptop would only display video on its own internal screen, not over HDMI, which required pointing an external camera at the laptop’s screen just to see what was happening during remote-controlled installation steps.
How does Linux performance compare to Windows and WSL?
This is where the story turns. With GPT-OSS-120B running on the GPU, Windows produced 65.4 tokens per second. WSL, which runs a Linux environment inside Windows, hit 65.1 tokens per second, nearly identical. The DGX Spark desktop unit, running Nvidia’s native Linux build, came in at 61 tokens per second. Native Linux on the laptop, however, dropped to 13.9 tokens per second, roughly five times slower.
Nothing gets lost.
The gap showed up again with vLLM running eight concurrent clients: WSL reached 127 tokens per second while native Linux reached 39.5. A longer benchmark run told the same story in time rather than throughput. Windows finished in about 8 minutes while holding the GPU near 2.2 GHz. Linux took 37 minutes, with the GPU parked around 790 MHz the entire time. Temperatures stayed low, between 40 and 47°C, so this isn’t a thermal throttling issue. The GPU simply isn’t being allowed to run at full speed.
Oddly, the direction of the problem flips depending on power source. Unplugged, Linux hit around 61 to 67 tokens per second on LM Studio, comparable to Windows. Plugged in, that same test dropped to about 15 tokens per second. Clock speed told the same story: around 1,800 MHz unplugged under load, and down to roughly 780 MHz when connected to wall power.
Why does plugging in the laptop slow Linux down?
The cause traces back to a component visible in Windows Device Manager called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework. This piece of firmware and driver logic manages the shared power budget between CPU and GPU, since a laptop (unlike the desktop DGX Spark) has to balance power delivery between both chips rather than feeding the GPU on its own line.
Disabling that controller in Windows reproduced the slowdown directly: tokens per second dropped from around 83 to about 31, and clock speed fell from roughly 2 GHz down to the same 786 MHz seen on Linux when plugged in. Re-enabling the controller restored normal speed immediately. That confirms the controller, not the kernel, the distribution, or the Nvidia GPU driver itself, is what’s holding Linux back.
The deeper issue is that the firmware hands this controller a table of power settings that is encrypted. Windows has the key to decrypt it. Linux currently does not, and no software fix attempted during testing could enable it, including one attempt that triggered a kernel panic. Extracting the decryption key from the Windows driver was floated as a theoretical workaround, but that would amount to a fragile, single-machine hack rather than something that works broadly. A real fix needs to come from Nvidia shipping equivalent power management logic in its Linux driver.
Is WSL a good substitute for native Linux right now?
For most developers, yes, at least for now. WSL runs on top of the Windows driver stack, so it inherits Windows’ full GPU boost behavior whether the laptop is plugged in or running on battery. It also runs Linux-first AI tools like vLLM and SGLang without the clock throttling problem that affects native Linux installs.
The one adjustment needed is memory. WSL reserves only 14GB by default, which isn’t enough for large model workloads on a 128GB unified memory machine, so that allocation needs to be increased manually. Once that’s done, WSL benchmarks land close to native Windows performance, making it the more practical choice until Nvidia addresses the Linux driver gap directly.
Frequently Asked Questions
Can the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop dual-boot Windows and Linux?
Yes. Dual-booting was demonstrated on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop using Omarchy, a Linux distribution that already included Nvidia’s open kernel driver for this chip, after an initial attempt with Debian required manual driver and networking workarounds.
Why is Linux so much slower than Windows on this laptop when plugged in?
● Reading src/server.ts
● Editing 3 files
+ import { limit } from 'rate'
- app.use(cors())
✓ Tests passed · ready for PR
A Windows-only firmware component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework manages power sharing between the CPU and GPU. Without a Linux equivalent, the GPU’s clock speed gets locked around 780 MHz when the laptop is connected to power, compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows.
Does unplugging the laptop fix the Linux performance problem?
It helps significantly. On battery power, Linux GPU clocks and token throughput come much closer to Windows levels. The severe slowdown specifically appears when the laptop is plugged into wall power, which is the opposite of what most users would expect.
Is WSL the same as running native Linux on the RTX Spark?
Not exactly, but it’s close in practice. WSL runs a Linux environment on top of the Windows kernel and driver stack, so it retains Windows’ GPU clock boost behavior and avoids the throttling issue, while still supporting Linux-native AI tools like vLLM.
Will Nvidia fix Linux GPU performance on RTX Spark laptops?
That depends on Nvidia shipping the platform controller’s power management logic in its Linux driver. The encrypted firmware power table currently can only be decrypted by Windows, and no workaround found so far restores full clock speed on Linux without it.

The lost malloc()
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
07:37:30 UTC
16:37:30 KST

The lost malloc()
(Sorry, I couldn't resist not putting a catchy title :)
Prompted by another project idea that popped into my mind, I did some Unix archaeology and looked at the original sources. This is the most fun I've ever had reading someone else's code - probably due to the historical significance. But also because of how delightfully approachable it was, compared to modern monstrocities.
This is a short(-ish) post regarding how they handled the mundane and boring task of allocating and managing memory (in C). In the future I'd like to read more about Unix the OS, its design, architecture & implementation.
A long time ago...
In a PDP far, far away, our journey begins with the fourth edition of Unix, released November '73, more than half a century ago. C actually first appeared in the second edition, released the year before, but wasn't extensively used. V4 is special because even the majority of the kernel was written in (let's call it "medieval") C by that point. The system had grown, however, and it was quite capable. You'll find that many Unix things we have today in POSIX-land were already present in V4.
Super fun fact: A tape containing V4 was only found last year! Previously, it was thought to be completely lost to time.
Linear allocation
The first interesting bit is found among the C "compiler" sources. In quotes, because it wasn't a monolithic compiler as we know it today. Rather, it was a set of distinct tools which you chained in order to get an object file from C code.
In /usr/c/c20.c:814, from what I can gather a very primitive optimiser, if you will (referred to as "C object code improver" in V5; there aren't many comments in V4) you see:
alloc(an)
{
    register int n;
    register char *p;
    n = an;
    n++;
    n =& ~01;
    if (lasta+n >= lastr) {
        if (sbrk(2000) == -1) {
            write(2, "Out of space\n", 14);
            exit(1);
        }
        lastr =+ 2000;
    }
    p = lasta;
    lasta =+ n;
    return(p);
}
Isn't that fascinating? This routine is used throughout the program to allocate memory. And if you squint, this is just a linear allocator. It aligns the size, checks if the region is big enough, otherwise tries to extend it. On failure, it just cold-exits. Which means callers don't have to check for NULL every single time, and indeed they do not.
The "region" isn't named, unlike how you'd do it today with arenas. However, the above does have a nice property, in that by using sbrk(), when we extend the heap, no pointer is invalidated.
And they don't bother freeing memory, because why would they? There's no need. Everything exists for the lifetime of the program.
dmr/malloc
This is the most interesting bit in my opinion, and the reason why I chose that title.
In Dennis' directory, you find a file named malloc.c. And you see two functions there:
struct map {
    char *m_size;
    char *m_addr;
};
malloc(mp, size)
struct map *mp;
mfree(mp, size, aa)
struct map *mp;
Seems familiar? Yep, it's mfree() with an m. These functions obviously deal with memory (de)allocation, and are the precursor to the ones we're familiar with today. But, the interfaces are different.
malloc() receives an additional first argument called mp (for "map"), and so does mfree(). What is that? Well, let's see how they're used:
p = malloc(coremap, sizeof foo);
...
mfree(coremap, sizeof foo, p);
q = malloc(swapmap, sizeof bar);
...
mfree(swapmap, sizeof bar, q);
So, they pass in some objects coremap and swapmap. What are those?
From /usr/sys/systm.h:2:
int	coremap[CMAPSIZ];
int	swapmap[SMAPSIZ];
They're just flat memory regions! So these malloc() and mfree() work on explicit memory regions! Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should. Those are just infinitely-times better interfaces than traditional malloc()/free().
Imagine using a library that has such an interface. You could deallocate all its memory resources by just discarding the entire region you delegated to it. Heap corruption bugs would be less severe because you could partition memory. You could trivially limit the amount of memory third party code allocates. The list goes on and on...
(Side note: They slightly messed up here and the regions should've been sized CMAPSIZ/2 and SMAPSIZ/2 respectively. They did fix that later.)
However, I don't think all these benefits were in the minds of Dennis and Ken. So why did they go with that interface and why did they partition memory to "core" and "swap"? The reason is, I believe, just hardware constraints. These interfaces stay like that up to V6 (maybe V7 too?), released the spring of '75, and thankfully there's an infamously good resource about that edition.
From A Commentary on the Sixth Edition UNIX Operating System by John Lions:
These are concerned with the allocation and subsequent release of two kinds of memory resources, namely:
- main memory in units of 32 words (64 bytes);
- disk swap area in units of 256 words (512 bytes).
For each of these two kinds of resource, a list of available areas is maintained within a resource "map" (either "coremap" or "swapmap"). A pointer to the appropriate resource "map" is always passed to "malloc" and "mfree" so that the routines themselves do not have to know the kind of resource with which they are dealing.
And it goes on to explain how the underlying allocation algorithm works. These do not do linear allocation (hence the mfree()). Basically, it's a list of blocks (struct map), ordered by address, where you do first-fit and also coalesce neighbour blocks.
The sixth edition is also the first where the term "arena" appears, in /usr/source/s4/alloc.s:17:
/char *allocs[2] {		/*initial empty arena*/
Rolling back
... to the topic of linear allocation... In V6's /usr/source/s1/diff1.c:88, I think the first ever version of diff(1), you find:
char *area;
char *top;
alloc(n)
{
    register char *p;
    p = area;
    n = (n+1) & ~1;
    area =+ n;
    while(area > top) {
        if(sbrk(1024) == -1) {
            mesg("Out of space\n");
            exit(1);
        }
        top =+ 1024;
    }
    return(p);
}
This is not all that much different from the previous alloc(), but this time it handles any allocation size. It uses a while to continue extending the region and stops when enough space has been reserved. The actual interesting part happens later, at unsort():143:
unsort(f, l, b)
struct line *f;
int *b;
{
    int *a;
    int i;
    a = alloc((l+1)*sizeof(a[0]));
    for(i=1;i<=l;i++)
        a[f[i].serial] = f[i].value;
    for(i=1;i<=l;i++)
        b[i] = a[i];
    area = a;
}
I'm not exactly sure what that function does, but it doesn't matter. What matters is that they allocate some memory (a = alloc(...);), then roll back the region (area = a;)! Though they subsequently just copy it to b, so it seems like this was redundant.
Computing sizes
Most of the code directly calls malloc()/alloc() and friends, and inlines the size computation logic. Like the line we saw earlier:
a = alloc((l+1)*sizeof(a[0]));
I don't do that anymore, and neither should you! I use a couple macros akin to C++'s new that handle all the sizeof business. But I am a dumb-dumb. Surely these guys must've come across the same pain points, and, if so, what did they do? Let's jump to V7, released January '79, four years after V6. You find this macro:
#define ALLOC(x) (struct x *) ckalloc(sizeof(struct x))
where they use it like:
struct foo { ... };
p = ALLOC(foo);
Nice! It's interesting to note where you find it; In /usr/src/cmd/f77/defines:38 and /usr/src/cmd/make/defs:38. Slightly suspicious. The former is part of the Fortran 77 compiler and latter of make. Stuart Feldman is the person who worked on both of those programs! It's clear that multiple people were working on the system at that time. A macro like that isn't used in any other program, sadly.
V7 is the first edition where you also find the assert() macro, and it was used extensively back then too. Good job! They also significantly expanded the number of man pages. Fun fact: I did $ man V7/usr/man/man3/foo.3 -- on 47 year old pages -- and it worked first try absolutely fine.
Let's go to V8, released in February '85, four years before the first C standard. You find this wild macro in /usr/src/cmd/ideal/memut.c:7:
char *fooalloc;
#define	tryalloc(new,kind)	\
    if (!(new =(kind *) malloc(sizeof (kind)))) {\
    emergency ();\
    if (!(new =(kind *) malloc(sizeof (kind)))) {\
        fprintf (stderr, "ideal: Out of space\n");\
        exit (1);\
        }\
    };\
    for (fooalloc = (char *) new;\
        fooalloc < ((char *) new) + sizeof (kind);\
        fooalloc ++)\
        *fooalloc = '\0';
If someone is too harsh because you used macros, point them at the above. Usage is bit different this time:
struct foo *x;
tryalloc(x, struct foo);
I decided to include it because the macro zero-initialises by default whatever was allocated! You also see a more familiar-looking malloc() being used. It appears this is the edition that they switched to the more traditional malloc()/free() interfaces we know. I'll hypothesize why that is at the very end.
But it gets even more interesting. In V8 you also find these macros:
#define new(type) ((type *) alloc (sizeof (type)))
#define new(t) ((t *) alloc (sizeof (t)))
#define        new(s)  (s *)alloc(sizeof (s))
When I saw these definitions I jumped out of my chair. It's basically how I'd define it too! You'll find them in:
- /usr/src/cmd/finddev.c:245, part of finddev(8).
- /usr/src/cmd/asd/asd.h:13, part of asd(8).
- /usr/include/ic.h:55, part of *checks notes* I have no idea.
respectively.
Unfortunately, I can't find the author(s) of any of these.
Cfront
In V8, you'll also find Cfront, a.k.a. medieval C++. It's then reasonable to assume that Stroustrup was inspired by the above macros and decided to incorporate new as a language-level feature. However, in A History of C++: 1979−1991, he writes:
In Simula, it is not possible to have local or global variables of class types; that is, every object of a class must be allocated on the free store using the new operator.
Huh. So C++'s new was inspired by the programming language "Simula". It's fair to say that the macros above were likely also derived from there. But Simula was quite old even by the 70s, let alone 1985. Perhaps Stroustrup persuaded people, or wrote those macros himself. He later writes:
The new operator that both allocates memory from the free store and invokes a constructor to ensure initialization was borrowed from Simula. The delete operator was a necessary complement because I did not want C with Classes to depend on a garbage collector. The argument for the new operator can be summarized like this. Would you rather write:
X* p = new X(2);
or
struct X * p = (struct X *) malloc(sizeof(struct X));
if (p == 0) error("memory exhausted");
p−>init(2);
and which version are you most likely to make a mistake in? The arguments against -- which were voiced quite a lot at the time -- were "but we don’t really need it," and "but someone will have used new as an identifier." Both observations are correct, of course. Introducing operator new thus made the use of free store more convenient and less error−prone. This increased its use even further so that the C free store allocation routine malloc() used to implement new became the most common performance bottleneck in real systems. [...] Having real programs spend 50% or more of their time in malloc() wasn’t acceptable.
(emphasis mine :P)
He makes a compelling argument, which I agree with, but doesn't mention the new() macros that basically did the same thing. Although you'll find many programs in V8 that do the latter, verbose thing. Now I want to know the author(s) of those macros even more!
Sims
This is a big parentheses because I wanted to know how Simula came up with new. Wikipedia states:
Simula 67 introduced objects, classes, inheritance and subclasses, virtual procedures, coroutines, and discrete event simulation, and featured garbage collection.
And it appeared in 1967. Wow! In the 1964 report of SIMULA I, you'll find:
[...] The symbol "new" only serves to resolve an ambiguity of the identifier A inside the activity blah blah blah [...]. Elsewhere the symbol new is redundant, but can often be used to advantage to improve readability.
So it was only used to resolve grammar ambiguities (I think?). And Stroustrup re-purposed it. Clever!
Further reading
The History of Simula, by Jan Rune Holmevik. Reads like (bad) Sci-Fi. All the politics nonsense aside, what I found most curious is that they completely specified the language before attempting to write a compiler for it. They started writing the first compiler atleast a year after. This would sound insane today, but I guess the cost of writing code was substantially higher back then.
Also: The development of the SIMULA languages, by the authors. I didn't read that one, although I should...
It's honestly amazing how influential Simula was. In "10.5 Operating Instruction" they even use the term "run time system" and give it the same meaning we're accustomed to.
Simula, in turn, was partly inspired by SIMSCRIPT (don't laugh). If you skim its 1962 report, you won't find a mention of new. You'll however find CREATE:
When a new Entity is created by a CREATE statement, space for storing its Attribute values is allocated in the amount specified on the Definition Form. This record is given an identification number, and the Variable specified in the CREATE statement is automatically set equal to this number.
For example, the statement "CREATE DOG CALLED FIDO" allocates the required amount of storage for the Attributes of a DOG, and sets FIDO equal to the identification number of the Attribute record.
Fascinating. The whole SIMSCRIPT report is fascinating actually, and I only briefly skimmed through it. At the beginning, it even describes something like a primitive ECS, by my understanding. At the end though it slaps you back to reality:
and you remember what year it was.
Later editions
In V9's /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:14, part of the Sam editor by Rob Pike, you find a "generalised" version of new():
#define    new(t, n)       ((t *)alloc(((ulong)(n)*sizeof(t))))
Although, by and large, almost every program doesn't do this. Most just directly call malloc() and friends, and do size calculations \w error checking at every call site. I don't know why, considering how much error-prone that is, but maybe due to inertia. It's a similar story in V10, but I didn't check it as thoroughly since it's quite big (it includes medieval GCC!).
So what happened?
They were so close to arenas; with linear allocation and explicit memory regions, rolling back, and even having a nice new() macro. All this is speculation at this point, but maybe some of it is correct. First of all, most programs had trivial object lifetimes. Allocate memory, read some data, process/crunch and spit out some result. You don't need any disciplined memory allocation strategy for that. You can even use malloc() for everything and let the OS reclaim it once the process exits. Given how simple malloc() was at first, it wouldn't be much of a bottleneck either. The philosophy of programs only "doing a single thing well" also fitted this pattern.
Secondly, it's clear some decisions were motivated by the very little memory they had to play with. And there was no virtual memory either (initially, that is). Nowadays, you can "allocate" however big of a memory region you want and all will probably be okay. They couldn't really do that, so they were fighting to reclaim every empty block and gap there was and scale a program's space with how much is actually needed. There's a counterpoint to this, however, because some code is confused. Sometimes you see fixed-size buffers/arrays pop up, seemingly out of nowhere, and the program bail out if they fill. I'm not sure why, but perhaps they didn't deem it worthwhile the complexity to use malloc() in those cases and/or "don't fix it if it ain't broke" kind-of thing.
And clearly, when they could get away with simple linear allocation, they did so.
Thirdly, I suspect they had grown tired of doing any manual memory management at all. Dropping explicit memory regions from the malloc() interface is a change that, on the surface, simplifies stuff even further. You make the implementation-side smarter and you don't have to worry about passing coremap or swapmap or anymap. Remember: the way programs and problems were approached didn't lead to complex object lifetimes. And when you had to deal with tangled lifetimes, malloc()/free() appear deceivably simple in the beginning.
That last point seems more "vibes" than evidence, but there is some evidence actually. In V7 they added galloc(3):
GALLOC(3)                                               GALLOC(3)
NAME
     galloc, gfree, garbage - storage allocation with garbage
     collection
SYNOPSIS
     char *galloc(n)
     unsigned n;
     gfree(p)
     char *p;
     garbage( )
DESCRIPTION
     These functions perform heap storage allocation with garbage
     collection.
     Galloc allocates a block of at least n bytes and returns a
     pointer to it.  Gfree frees a block previously allocated by
     galloc.
     When space gets tight, garbage blocks are freed automati-
     cally.  A block allocated by galloc is deemed to be garbage
     unless it is reachable.  A reachable block is one whose
     first byte is pointed to by a declared C variable or by a
     pointer in a reachable block.
and Rob Pike had this in /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:15:
#define    gcnew(p, n)     ((void)gcalloc((ulong)(n)*sizeof((p)[0]), (long **)&(p)))
Ha, myth busted! The authors and people closest to C wanted garbage collection. Given how fast computers are -- and the pace of that -- this makes sense. It's even clearer if you look at what they did later with Limbo and Go. They wanted a higher level general purpose language to write programs in. They had C, so they tried to bolt GC on top of that.
Lastly, I should note that many of these problems were largely known, even at the time. In The Standard C library (1992), P. J. Plauger writes:
Allocating and freeing data objects on the heap in arbitrary order inevitably leaves unusable holes between some of the allocated data objects. That too lowers the usable size of the heap.
Don't overreact to this knowledge. Gather related data into a structure and allocate it all at once. That minimizes heap overhead, to be sure, but it is also good programming style. Do not gather unrelated data just to save heap overhead. Similarly, allocate data objects with similar lifetimes all at once, then free them at about the same time. That minimizes heap fragmentation, but it too is good style. Do not advance or defer unrelated heap operations just to minimize fragmentation. The storage allocation functions are an important aid to programming flexibility. Use them as they are intended to be used.
Criticism by yours truly: It's much easier to say "just do the right thing™" than show and provide tools for how to actually do it.
Conclusion
I don't know. Pay attention to good ideas, otherwise they might get lost? (literally in the case of V4, lol) Sounds cheesy.
Also, the "C object code improver" shatters the illusion that C was somehow magically fast. In fact, Ritchie later added an expression optimiser, and they kept extending both in each edition. I think C just wasn't slow, and it was made fast only with engineering effort put into the compiler (and even then, they had to add register because the compiler wasn't that smart either). It probably remained fast because Unix spread quickly and it carried C along with it, so hardware manufacturers adapted to C. There's a nice essay by Mike Pall discussing how modern CPUs try very hard to infer invariants from compiled C code (which the compiler tried very hard to optimise) and the costs associated with that.
At one point, I also want to investigate Inferno and Plan 9 more. Maybe the BSDs too. Until then...
Cya!

The lost malloc()
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
07:37:30 UTC
16:37:30 KST

The lost malloc()
(Sorry, I couldn't resist not putting a catchy title :)
Prompted by another project idea that popped into my mind, I did some Unix archaeology and looked at the original sources. This is the most fun I've ever had reading someone else's code - probably due to the historical significance. But also because of how delightfully approachable it was, compared to modern monstrocities.
This is a short(-ish) post regarding how they handled the mundane and boring task of allocating and managing memory (in C). In the future I'd like to read more about Unix the OS, its design, architecture & implementation.
A long time ago...
In a PDP far, far away, our journey begins with the fourth edition of Unix, released November '73, more than half a century ago. C actually first appeared in the second edition, released the year before, but wasn't extensively used. V4 is special because even the majority of the kernel was written in (let's call it "medieval") C by that point. The system had grown, however, and it was quite capable. You'll find that many Unix things we have today in POSIX-land were already present in V4.
Super fun fact: A tape containing V4 was only found last year! Previously, it was thought to be completely lost to time.
Linear allocation
The first interesting bit is found among the C "compiler" sources. In quotes, because it wasn't a monolithic compiler as we know it today. Rather, it was a set of distinct tools which you chained in order to get an object file from C code.
In /usr/c/c20.c:814, from what I can gather a very primitive optimiser, if you will (referred to as "C object code improver" in V5; there aren't many comments in V4) you see:
alloc(an)
{
    register int n;
    register char *p;
    n = an;
    n++;
    n =& ~01;
    if (lasta+n >= lastr) {
        if (sbrk(2000) == -1) {
            write(2, "Out of space\n", 14);
            exit(1);
        }
        lastr =+ 2000;
    }
    p = lasta;
    lasta =+ n;
    return(p);
}
Isn't that fascinating? This routine is used throughout the program to allocate memory. And if you squint, this is just a linear allocator. It aligns the size, checks if the region is big enough, otherwise tries to extend it. On failure, it just cold-exits. Which means callers don't have to check for NULL every single time, and indeed they do not.
The "region" isn't named, unlike how you'd do it today with arenas. However, the above does have a nice property, in that by using sbrk(), when we extend the heap, no pointer is invalidated.
And they don't bother freeing memory, because why would they? There's no need. Everything exists for the lifetime of the program.
dmr/malloc
This is the most interesting bit in my opinion, and the reason why I chose that title.
In Dennis' directory, you find a file named malloc.c. And you see two functions there:
struct map {
    char *m_size;
    char *m_addr;
};
malloc(mp, size)
struct map *mp;
mfree(mp, size, aa)
struct map *mp;
Seems familiar? Yep, it's mfree() with an m. These functions obviously deal with memory (de)allocation, and are the precursor to the ones we're familiar with today. But, the interfaces are different.
malloc() receives an additional first argument called mp (for "map"), and so does mfree(). What is that? Well, let's see how they're used:
p = malloc(coremap, sizeof foo);
...
mfree(coremap, sizeof foo, p);
q = malloc(swapmap, sizeof bar);
...
mfree(swapmap, sizeof bar, q);
So, they pass in some objects coremap and swapmap. What are those?
From /usr/sys/systm.h:2:
int	coremap[CMAPSIZ];
int	swapmap[SMAPSIZ];
They're just flat memory regions! So these malloc() and mfree() work on explicit memory regions! Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should. Those are just infinitely-times better interfaces than traditional malloc()/free().
Imagine using a library that has such an interface. You could deallocate all its memory resources by just discarding the entire region you delegated to it. Heap corruption bugs would be less severe because you could partition memory. You could trivially limit the amount of memory third party code allocates. The list goes on and on...
(Side note: They slightly messed up here and the regions should've been sized CMAPSIZ/2 and SMAPSIZ/2 respectively. They did fix that later.)
However, I don't think all these benefits were in the minds of Dennis and Ken. So why did they go with that interface and why did they partition memory to "core" and "swap"? The reason is, I believe, just hardware constraints. These interfaces stay like that up to V6 (maybe V7 too?), released the spring of '75, and thankfully there's an infamously good resource about that edition.
From A Commentary on the Sixth Edition UNIX Operating System by John Lions:
These are concerned with the allocation and subsequent release of two kinds of memory resources, namely:
- main memory in units of 32 words (64 bytes);
- disk swap area in units of 256 words (512 bytes).
For each of these two kinds of resource, a list of available areas is maintained within a resource "map" (either "coremap" or "swapmap"). A pointer to the appropriate resource "map" is always passed to "malloc" and "mfree" so that the routines themselves do not have to know the kind of resource with which they are dealing.
And it goes on to explain how the underlying allocation algorithm works. These do not do linear allocation (hence the mfree()). Basically, it's a list of blocks (struct map), ordered by address, where you do first-fit and also coalesce neighbour blocks.
The sixth edition is also the first where the term "arena" appears, in /usr/source/s4/alloc.s:17:
/char *allocs[2] {		/*initial empty arena*/
Rolling back
... to the topic of linear allocation... In V6's /usr/source/s1/diff1.c:88, I think the first ever version of diff(1), you find:
char *area;
char *top;
alloc(n)
{
    register char *p;
    p = area;
    n = (n+1) & ~1;
    area =+ n;
    while(area > top) {
        if(sbrk(1024) == -1) {
            mesg("Out of space\n");
            exit(1);
        }
        top =+ 1024;
    }
    return(p);
}
This is not all that much different from the previous alloc(), but this time it handles any allocation size. It uses a while to continue extending the region and stops when enough space has been reserved. The actual interesting part happens later, at unsort():143:
unsort(f, l, b)
struct line *f;
int *b;
{
    int *a;
    int i;
    a = alloc((l+1)*sizeof(a[0]));
    for(i=1;i<=l;i++)
        a[f[i].serial] = f[i].value;
    for(i=1;i<=l;i++)
        b[i] = a[i];
    area = a;
}
I'm not exactly sure what that function does, but it doesn't matter. What matters is that they allocate some memory (a = alloc(...);), then roll back the region (area = a;)! Though they subsequently just copy it to b, so it seems like this was redundant.
Computing sizes
Most of the code directly calls malloc()/alloc() and friends, and inlines the size computation logic. Like the line we saw earlier:
a = alloc((l+1)*sizeof(a[0]));
I don't do that anymore, and neither should you! I use a couple macros akin to C++'s new that handle all the sizeof business. But I am a dumb-dumb. Surely these guys must've come across the same pain points, and, if so, what did they do? Let's jump to V7, released January '79, four years after V6. You find this macro:
#define ALLOC(x) (struct x *) ckalloc(sizeof(struct x))
where they use it like:
struct foo { ... };
p = ALLOC(foo);
Nice! It's interesting to note where you find it; In /usr/src/cmd/f77/defines:38 and /usr/src/cmd/make/defs:38. Slightly suspicious. The former is part of the Fortran 77 compiler and latter of make. Stuart Feldman is the person who worked on both of those programs! It's clear that multiple people were working on the system at that time. A macro like that isn't used in any other program, sadly.
V7 is the first edition where you also find the assert() macro, and it was used extensively back then too. Good job! They also significantly expanded the number of man pages. Fun fact: I did $ man V7/usr/man/man3/foo.3 -- on 47 year old pages -- and it worked first try absolutely fine.
Let's go to V8, released in February '85, four years before the first C standard. You find this wild macro in /usr/src/cmd/ideal/memut.c:7:
char *fooalloc;
#define	tryalloc(new,kind)	\
    if (!(new =(kind *) malloc(sizeof (kind)))) {\
    emergency ();\
    if (!(new =(kind *) malloc(sizeof (kind)))) {\
        fprintf (stderr, "ideal: Out of space\n");\
        exit (1);\
        }\
    };\
    for (fooalloc = (char *) new;\
        fooalloc < ((char *) new) + sizeof (kind);\
        fooalloc ++)\
        *fooalloc = '\0';
If someone is too harsh because you used macros, point them at the above. Usage is bit different this time:
struct foo *x;
tryalloc(x, struct foo);
I decided to include it because the macro zero-initialises by default whatever was allocated! You also see a more familiar-looking malloc() being used. It appears this is the edition that they switched to the more traditional malloc()/free() interfaces we know. I'll hypothesize why that is at the very end.
But it gets even more interesting. In V8 you also find these macros:
#define new(type) ((type *) alloc (sizeof (type)))
#define new(t) ((t *) alloc (sizeof (t)))
#define        new(s)  (s *)alloc(sizeof (s))
When I saw these definitions I jumped out of my chair. It's basically how I'd define it too! You'll find them in:
- /usr/src/cmd/finddev.c:245, part of finddev(8).
- /usr/src/cmd/asd/asd.h:13, part of asd(8).
- /usr/include/ic.h:55, part of *checks notes* I have no idea.
respectively.
Unfortunately, I can't find the author(s) of any of these.
Cfront
In V8, you'll also find Cfront, a.k.a. medieval C++. It's then reasonable to assume that Stroustrup was inspired by the above macros and decided to incorporate new as a language-level feature. However, in A History of C++: 1979−1991, he writes:
In Simula, it is not possible to have local or global variables of class types; that is, every object of a class must be allocated on the free store using the new operator.
Huh. So C++'s new was inspired by the programming language "Simula". It's fair to say that the macros above were likely also derived from there. But Simula was quite old even by the 70s, let alone 1985. Perhaps Stroustrup persuaded people, or wrote those macros himself. He later writes:

The delete operator was a necessary complement because I did not want C with Classes to depend on a garbage collector. The argument for the new operator can be summarized like this. Would you rather write:
X* p = new X(2);
or
struct X * p = (struct X *) malloc(sizeof(struct X));
if (p == 0) error("memory exhausted");
p−>init(2);
and which version are you most likely to make a mistake in? The arguments against -- which were voiced quite a lot at the time -- were "but we don’t really need it," and "but someone will have used new as an identifier." Both observations are correct, of course. Introducing operator new thus made the use of free store more convenient and less error−prone. This increased its use even further so that the C free store allocation routine malloc() used to implement new became the most common performance bottleneck in real systems. [...] Having real programs spend 50% or more of their time in malloc() wasn’t acceptable.
(emphasis mine :P)
He makes a compelling argument, which I agree with, but doesn't mention the new() macros that basically did the same thing. Although you'll find many programs in V8 that do the latter, verbose thing. Now I want to know the author(s) of those macros even more!

And it appeared in 1967. Wow! In the 1964 report of SIMULA I, you'll find:

Further reading
The History of Simula, by Jan Rune Holmevik. Reads like (bad) Sci-Fi. Fascinating. The whole SIMSCRIPT report is fascinating actually, and I only briefly skimmed through it. At the beginning, it even describes something like a primitive ECS, by my understanding. At the end though it slaps you back to reality:
and you remember what year it was.
Later editions
In V9's /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:14, part of the Sam editor by Rob Pike, you find a "generalised" version of new():

And clearly, when they could get away with simple linear allocation, they did so.
Thirdly, I suspect they had grown tired of doing any manual memory management at all. Dropping explicit memory regions from the malloc() interface is a change that, on the surface, simplifies stuff even further. You make the implementation-side smarter and you don't have to worry about passing coremap or swapmap or anymap. Remember: the way programs and problems were approached didn't lead to complex object lifetimes. And when you had to deal with tangled lifetimes, malloc()/free() appear deceivably simple in the beginning.
That last point seems more "vibes" than evidence, but there is some evidence actually. In V7 they added galloc(3):
GALLOC(3)                                               GALLOC(3)
NAME
     galloc, gfree, garbage - storage allocation with garbage
     collection
SYNOPSIS
     char *galloc(n)
     unsigned n;
     gfree(p)
     char *p;
     garbage( )
DESCRIPTION
     These functions perform heap storage allocation with garbage
     collection.
     Galloc allocates a block of at least n bytes and returns a
     pointer to it.  Gfree frees a block previously allocated by
     galloc.
     When space gets tight, garbage blocks are freed automati-
     cally.  A block allocated by galloc is deemed to be garbage
     unless it is reachable.  A reachable block is one whose
     first byte is pointed to by a declared C variable or by a
     pointer in a reachable block.
and Rob Pike had this in /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:15:
#define    gcnew(p, n)     ((void)gcalloc((ulong)(n)*sizeof((p)[0]), (long **)&(p)))
Ha, myth busted! The authors and people closest to C wanted garbage collection. Given how fast computers are -- and the pace of that -- this makes sense. It's even clearer if you look at what they did later with Limbo and Go. They wanted a higher level general purpose language to write programs in. They had C, so they tried to bolt GC on top of that.
Lastly, I should note that many of these problems were largely known, even at the time. In The Standard C library (1992), P. J. Plauger writes:
Allocating and freeing data objects on the heap in arbitrary order inevitably leaves unusable holes between some of the allocated data objects. That too lowers the usable size of the heap.
Don't overreact to this knowledge. Gather related data into a structure and allocate it all at once. That minimizes heap overhead, to be sure, but it is also good programming style. Do not gather unrelated data just to save heap overhead. Similarly, allocate data objects with similar lifetimes all at once, then free them at about the same time. That minimizes heap fragmentation, but it too is good style. Do not advance or defer unrelated heap operations just to minimize fragmentation. The storage allocation functions are an important aid to programming flexibility. Use them as they are intended to be used.
Criticism by yours truly: It's much easier to say "just do the right thing™" than show and provide tools for how to actually do it.
Conclusion
I don't know. Pay attention to good ideas, otherwise they might get lost? (literally in the case of V4, lol) Sounds cheesy.
Also, the "C object code improver" shatters the illusion that C was somehow magically fast. In fact, Ritchie later added an expression optimiser, and they kept extending both in each edition. I think C just wasn't slow, and it was made fast only with engineering effort put into the compiler (and even then, they had to add register because the compiler wasn't that smart either). It probably remained fast because Unix spread quickly and it carried C along with it, so hardware manufacturers adapted to C. There's a nice essay by Mike Pall discussing how modern CPUs try very hard to infer invariants from compiled C code (which the compiler tried very hard to optimise) and the costs associated with that.
At one point, I also want to investigate Inferno and Plan 9 more. Maybe the BSDs too. Until then...
Cya!

Democrats Rout GOP

Democrats Seize Control of Congress as Voters Rebuke Trump
Democrats flipped seven Senate seats, including three in states held by Republicans for decades, and overcame a redistricting effort to capture the House. President Trump told The New York Times that he would accept the election results.
Latest
Democrats seized control of the Senate and the House as voters delivered a blistering rebuke to President Trump in a midterm rout that reset the balance of power in Washington. The romp stretched from coast to coast, with Democrats flipping seats that had spent decades in Republican hands and taking House districts in corners of the country that had long seemed inaccessible.
Mr. Trump told The Times in an interview that he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” and was prepared to work with Democrats. “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them,” he said. “We’ll probably work something out.”
Voters swept out Republican candidates who tethered themselves to Mr. Trump and those who sought a modicum of independence from him. Democrats flipped Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and even Texas, according to The Associated Press. Many of those states had been longtime conservative strongholds. Republicans had held the Senate seats in Texas and South Carolina for decades. The Kansas seat had been red for nearly a century.
Senator Susan Collins, a Maine Republican who across 30 years in Washington repeatedly foiled Democratic efforts to unseat her, conceded her race to Troy Jackson, a former state legislator whom Democrats anointed in July after their preferred nominee quit the race in scandal.
In Texas, James Talarico, a state legislator who became a national fund-raising sensation, toppled Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden Republican state attorney general whom Mr. Trump elevated to the nomination in the spring.
“We just took back Texas,” Mr. Talarico said in his victory speech. “We just showed that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love.”
In South Carolina, Dr. Annie Andrews prevailed over Senator Darline Graham, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. In Kansas, the Rev. Adam Hamilton stunned Senator Roger Marshall, a one-term Republican.
And Dr. Abdul El-Sayed prevailed in Michigan even after his Senate campaign was rattled on Sunday when his defeated primary rival, Representative Haley Stevens, endorsed the Republican nominee and drew the scorn of her own party.
Democrats could still widen their lead in the Senate: Ballots were still being counted in Alaska, where Republicans have complained that a potential spoiler candidate could unfairly siphon votes from their incumbent, and in Mississippi, an unlikely battleground where a couple dozen votes separated the two candidates.
Democrats also notched major victories in races for governor. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman to be elected governor in the country’s history. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa was the first Democrat elected governor since Ann Richards in 1990, by ousting Gov. Greg Abbott, a three-term Republican.
In another race for governor, Dr. Amy Acton became the first woman elected to lead Ohio, emerging from a vicious campaign that included an ad by her Republican opponent that featured her estranged mother. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat ousted from his seat two years ago, will again represent Ohio in the Senate after flipping a Republican seat.
The results came in a midterm election that is the first national mandate on Mr. Trump’s second term. They showed what polls have indicated for months — that voters are supremely dissatisfied with Mr. Trump and Republicans who have backed his agenda.
Democrats flipped House seats across the map. And the redistricting effort Republicans undertook in hopes of protecting their majority failed to yield victories that they intended: Democrats won districts in Florida that Republicans redrew to be favorable for themselves, and a North Carolina seat Democrats flipped was also part of the Republican redistricting effort.
Democratic candidates have blamed Mr. Trump, and the war he started this year in Iran, for the economic hardships that have driven a current of frustration across the nation. Republicans have focused on portraying their Democratic opponents as extreme on social issues and the economy as they played defense in reliably red states.
Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida: Senator Ashley Moody defeated Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat, in a tight contest to complete the term of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The last polling places closed at 1 a.m. Eastern on Wednesday, in Alaska, and full results for some races may not be known for days or longer.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
- A complicated landscape: More than 400 Times reporters, editors, data analysts, video journalists and photographers are covering the midterms, seeking to understand a large country with voters who are complicated — and sometimes contradictory. Read more ›
- Minor disruptions: A technical problem with voting machines in Westchester County, N.Y., outside New York City, led officials there to collect ballots by hand in a competitive House race. In Florida, flooding forced more than 20 polling stations across eight counties to be relocated. In North Carolina, technical problems at several precincts caused minor delays; state election officials said they would delay the release of election results to at least 8:15 p.m. from 7:30 p.m. Read more ›
- Election integrity: Many election officials and Democrats have said they fear that Mr. Trump’s attacks on the integrity of U.S. elections could lead to tensions during voting and baseless challenges to the outcome. The administration has sought to prove that many noncitizens have cast ballots, but few people have been charged with offenses related to voting fraud. Local and state officials say they are well prepared to run a secure election.
- Court rulings: A federal judge has turned down a request by Democratic lawmakers and party organizations to prohibit the Trump administration from coercing states into screening incoming ballots. And the Supreme Court issued what appeared to be an extraordinary rebuke to Mr. Trump, signaling that it was not interested in assisting his efforts to interfere with how states administer elections.
Gov. Tina Kotek, one of the few endangered Democratic incumbents in a difficult year for Republicans, prevailed in her re-election bid, The Associated Press said, as she was powered in the end by a pro-Democratic environment in her blue state.
Ms. Kotek, who had been the longest-serving House speaker in Oregon history before winning the governorship four years ago, defeated State Senator Christine Drazan, the same Republican she beat in her first run for governor.
Ms. Kotek ran in 2022 pledging to reduce homelessness, expand access to addiction and mental health services, supercharge housing production and improve public schools. Progress on all of those issues has been far slower than promised.
In 2024, she faced an ethics controversy over her efforts to give her wife an expanded role in state government, prompting the departure of three top aides and forcing the governor to abandon her plans and apologize. A state ethics commission later dismissed complaints against her.
Liberal Democrats in Oregon have been frustrated by Ms. Kotek’s efforts to woo business leaders and work with Republicans. The state’s largest teachers union, a traditional source of Democratic support and get-out-the-vote efforts, opted not to endorse in the race.
Recent polls have shown Ms. Kotek’s dissatisfaction ratings rivaling those of President Trump.
