Nebraska voters rejected two ballot measures that would have legalized online sports betting in the state. Gambling companies supporting the measures, including DraftKings and FanDuel, poured more than $20 million into the campaign, promising new tax revenue for property tax relief. Opponents, who raised just over $1 million, warned that online betting would threaten the integrity of college sports and fuel gambling addiction.
Arizona voters have approved a ballot measure barring transgender student athletes from participating on teams that match their gender identity, The Associated Press reported. The measure also requires transgender students to use only those restrooms and locker rooms that match their sex at birth.
Senator Pete Ricketts, a Nebraska Republican backed by President Trump, won re-election on Wednesday, according to The Associated Press, staving off a competitive challenge from an independent candidate with a working-class platform.
Mr. Ricketts’s victory against Dan Osborn, a mechanic and military veteran who ran without party affiliation, confirmed the strength of the Republican Party and the senator’s conservative record in the deep-red state despite the growing discontent with Mr. Trump’s economic policies.
Mr. Ricketts focused his campaign on his reliably conservative record in his years of public service in Nebraska and reiterated his focus on border security and economic support for farmers. He has acknowledged the financial strain that the Iran war has brought to Nebraska families and farmers by raising fuel and fertilizer prices, but he has not opposed the conflict.
Mr. Osborn’s independent status appealed to swing voters, Democrats and Republicans disillusioned with the Trump administration. He was also aided when the Democratic nominee, Cindy Burbank, withdrew from the race, backing Mr. Osborn believing that he would have a better chance of unseating Mr. Ricketts.
But Mr. Ricketts’s deep ties to Nebraska, name recognition as a former governor and Republican allegiance in a red state proved too much for Mr. Osborn to overcome.
Before being appointed to the Senate in 2023, Mr. Ricketts served two terms as governor. Across those roles, he has delivered tax cuts, supported the agriculture industry, pushed business-friendly policies and promoted securing the southern border.
Mr. Ricketts comes from a powerful family in Nebraska politics. His father, Joe Ricketts, is a Republican megadonor and billionaire businessman and founded the brokerage firm TD Ameritrade.
The senator previously worked in executive roles at the firm, and served as a board member of the Chicago Cubs, which he partly owns.
Two traditionally stalwart Democratic groups returned to the party fold these midterms after a dalliance with the G.O.P. in 2024.
Counties with a Black majority had drifted a little more than a percentage point toward Trump two years ago. But when the dust settled this election night, those places moved nearly 16 percentage points toward Democratic Senate candidates. The Democrats ended up beating their Republican opponents by more than 50 percentage points in some counties.
Young voters also appear to have come back to the Democratic fold after some signs they were willing to vote Republican. After counties with large numbers of 18- to 34-year-olds swung more than seven percentage points to Mr. Trump in 2024, they swerved left by nearly 23 percentage points this year.
Gov. Katie Hobbs, one of the most vulnerable Democratic incumbents in the 2026 election year, held on to Arizona’s highest office for another four years, The Associated Press said, solidifying Democratic leadership of the swing state heading into the 2028 presidential election.
Ms. Hobbs, a moderate, defeated Representative Andy Biggs, an ally of President Trump’s who had the backing of Turning Point USA, the conservative organization founded by Charlie Kirk. Her victory represents the latest rebuke of far-right Republicans in Arizona, and it was the first time in two decades that a Democratic governor won re-election in the state.
Ms. Hobbs campaigned for the support of independents, who make up Arizona’s largest share of registered voters, and moderate Republicans. She even tapped a former Republican, John Giles, the former mayor of the city of Mesa, as her running mate.
Ms. Hobbs campaigned on affordability and protection of the drought-stricken state’s water. Though her refusal to debate Mr. Biggs earned her derision, the decision was validated by her victory.
In 2022, Ms. Hobbs barely edged out a far-right firebrand, Kari Lake, who lost in a U.S. Senate bid two years later. Mr. Biggs tried to make the case that he was a more electable Republican, but Democrats framed him otherwise, slamming his efforts to overturn the 2020 election and claiming that he turned a blind eye to child abuse by a Mormon splinter group more than a decade ago as president of the State Senate.
Turning Point PAC Arizona, a political arm of Turning Point USA, dumped nearly $20 million in support of Mr. Biggs’s campaign this year, but he was still outspent by Ms. Hobbs.
For Democrats hoping to retake the White House in 2028, Ms. Hobbs’s presence in the governor’s office will come as a relief. The state has been a hotbed of election deniers since Joseph R. Biden Jr. narrowly won it in 2020, and Democrats feared Mr. Biggs would empower those who still claim wrongly that Mr. Trump has won the state three times.
With Democrats performing so well around the country, the party will be looking at Montana as a big potential missed opportunity. For months, supporters of Seth Bodnar, a well-funded left-leaning independent, and Alani Bankhead, the little-known Democratic nominee, feuded with each other and tried to pressure each other to drop out of the race. In the end, neither did and they split Democratic votes, helping Kurt Alme, the Republican, to an easy victory.
Dan S. Sullivan’s lead in Alaska’s Senate race masks the fact that he is underperforming President Trump’s margins in the 2024 race. Much of the reported vote is from ballots cast on Election Day, which are favorable for Republicans. In the 27 districts that have finished tallying such votes, Sullivan is running behind Trump by an average of 12 percentage points.
In District 22, which includes North Muldoon, one of the most diverse areas in the state, Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate, leads by nearly 20 percentage points among Election Day voters. Trump carried the same district’s day-of vote by nearly four points in 2024. The remaining votes here will be from early and mail ballots, which are expected to lean toward Peltola.
Beau Bayh, a Democrat, was elected Indiana secretary of state, The Associated Press reported, ending a Republican lockout on all statewide offices. Bayh, a Marine veteran and lawyer, is a son of former Senator Evan Bayh of Indiana. The Republican incumbent, Diego Morales, did not receive his party’s nomination for another term.
It’s after midnight in Los Angeles. While the Associated Press has not yet called the city’s mayoral race, Nithya Raman, the D.S.A.-aligned challenger to Mayor Karen Bass, gave a speech that sounded a lot like a victory address. She told the crowd of supporters, who were buzzing about progressive wins across the country, that she was hopeful. “But I’m also really superstitious,” she said, “so we’re all just gonna be cool, OK?”
Kurt Alme, a former federal prosecutor, won the Senate race in Montana, according to The Associated Press, allowing Republicans to hold on to an open seat in conservative territory. Alme, the former U.S. attorney for Montana, focused his campaign on reducing federal spending and bringing tax relief.
He entered the race in March after Senator Steve Daines withdrew his candidacy just minutes before the filing deadline. Daines and Gov. Greg Gianforte, a Republican, quickly endorsed Alme, as did President Trump. Some Democrats backed the independent bid of Seth Bodnar over their own nominee, Alani Bankhead, believing he was more electable in the heavily Republican state, and Alme was able to capitalize on the rift.
Representative Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, the longest-serving woman in Congress, defeated Derek Merrin, a Republican, according to The Associated Press, to win her 23rd term. Kaptur, 80, was first elected to the House in 1982. She edged out Merrin two years ago in an area that President Trump carried, and the Ninth Congressional District was redrawn to tilt more conservative. Kaptur prepared for the rematch by moderating her stances to defend her seat. She faced local Democratic backlash over an ad in which she said that “boys should not play in girls’ sports.”
Voters in Idaho, one of the country’s most conservative states, turned back an effort to repeal the state’s abortion ban, according to The Associated Press.
Two years before the Supreme Court overturned the constitutional right to an abortion, Idaho lawmakers had already passed a ban, making it a crime for doctors or other health care professionals to terminate a pregnancy. The law went into effect when the high court reversed itself on Roe v. Wade.
Since then, in-person abortions have nearly vanished in Idaho, but the state has also experienced a dramatic drop in the number of doctors practicing obstetrics. A study published last year found that Idaho had lost 94 of the 268 physicians who were practicing obstetrics when the ban took effect, a 35 percent decline in the first two years, even after accounting for doctors who had arrived in the state over that time. About half of Idaho’s 44 counties lack a practicing obstetrician-gynecologist.
Proponents of repealing the ban argued that the state’s Republican-dominated Legislature had gone too far with a law that led to long wait times and fear among the doctors who have stayed. They hoped that Idaho would join Kansas and Missouri, other conservative states where voters have rolled back abortion limits.
Conservatives and the Idaho Republican Party made maintaining the ban their big issue and used it to drive voter turnout. They said the statistics about doctors fleeing the state were overblown, noting the number of people with active obstetrician and gynecologist licenses in Idaho grew since the abortion ban. Doctors do not need to live or practice full time in the state to maintain one, and not all OB-GYN practices offer a full range of women’s health care.
Opponents of the referendum also focused on aspects of the measure that went beyond abortion. The proposition would have also enshrined a right to birth control and fertility treatments in Idaho.
Attorney General Keith Ellison of Minnesota, a Democrat, won a third term, The Associated Press reported, fending off a challenge from a trial lawyer who sought to portray him as complicit in the proliferation of fraud in state-run welfare programs.
Ellison touted the lawsuits his office had filed against the Trump administration, including over its immigration enforcement and pursuit of voter data. He warned that his opponent, Ron Schutz, would be a rubber stamp for the White House.
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat and outspoken critic of Israel, won Michigan’s Senate race, according to The Associated Press, maintaining his party’s hold on a crucial battleground seat despite a remarkable last-minute defection from his rival in the primary.
Dr. El-Sayed, 42, will become the nation’s first Muslim senator when he is seated in January. He defeated former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican making his second run for the Senate, in a campaign that became one of the country’s most bitter and expensive contests.
Dr. El-Sayed overcame opposition not only from Republicans, but also, in the final days, from Representative Haley Stevens, the moderate Democrat he beat in the primary. On Sunday, after days of growing criticism of Dr. El-Sayed, she rescinded her support of the Democrat and made a stunning endorsement of Mr. Rogers.
Her late opposition was emblematic of a faction of moderate Democrats and Jewish voters who found Dr. El-Sayed’s position on Israel untenable. In the end, though, Ms. Stevens proved to have a limited constituency. Her endorsement of Mr. Rogers drew broad condemnation across the Democratic Party.
Dr. El-Sayed’s triumph gives Democrats a critical victory and keeps them in control of the seat held by Senator Gary Peters, who is retiring.
A talented orator and debater, Dr. El-Sayed ran on a platform of “money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all.” He focused relentlessly on tying Mr. Rogers to President Trump and his policies, especially the war in Iran and tariffs, which have driven up prices. He also reveled in schoolyard taunts, calling Mr. Rogers “a beta” during a Fox News appearance.
But throughout his campaign, questions lingered over whether he could win over crucial segments of Democrats’ traditional base. Black voters, especially in Detroit, have long had tensions with Arab Americans in the region.
And suburban Jewish voters who have been loyal Democrats for generations blanched at his suggestions that Israel should not exist as an explicitly Jewish state — a position he had softened by the end of his campaign — and that the United States should cut off military aid to the country.
In the campaign’s final weeks, Dr. El-Sayed faced a blitz of Republican attacks centered on his faith and family. At televised debates, Mr. Rogers questioned Dr. El-Sayed’s loyalty to America, invoked his mother and suggested he was in league with the Muslim Brotherhood, the Islamist political movement. (Dr. El-Sayed has disavowed the movement.)
Mr. Trump called Dr. El-Sayed a “jihadist” at a rally last month in Port Huron, Mich., and in Truth Social posts.
Throughout the campaign, Dr. El-Sayed emerged as a litmus test for Democrats. Progressives argued that his muscular left-wing politics were the party’s future and sought to cast his campaign as an example for others to follow. But centrist and moderate Democrats who backed Ms. Stevens in the primary saw his approach as an unnecessary risk in a battleground state.
Late in the race, a low-grade feud between Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed exploded into public view. Ms. Stevens had spent the campaign’s final weeks offering increasingly pointed criticism about Dr. El-Sayed’s position on Israel and demanding that he condemn an online ad made by an outside group that supported him. Dr. El-Sayed publicly uninvited Ms. Stevens from a planned joint appearance at a Detroit church; Ms. Stevens responded by pulling her endorsement and backing Mr. Rogers.
Dr. El-Sayed has telegraphed high ambitions in the Senate.
He has said he aims to influence Democratic policy on health care and Israel, both in Washington and during the 2028 presidential contest. Michigan is set to play a newly influential role in the party’s primary race, with the Democratic National Committee placing the state fifth on its revamped calendar.
Leading liberal figures flooded into the state to campaign for Dr. El-Sayed. Former President Barack Obama held a rally in Detroit for him, and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York accompanied him for a day of campaign stops. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont held rallies to try to juice turnout for him.
The Senate race was the most expensive in state history, with $278 million spent on television and digital advertising, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm. Dr. El-Sayed was outspent in both the Democratic primary, when pro-Israel super PACs supported Ms. Stevens, and during the general election against Mr. Rogers.
There are still no results in Nevada, more than four hours after polls closed there. That’s because, per state law, no results can be reported until the last person who was in line to vote before polls closed has gotten a chance to cast a ballot — and exceptionally long lines in Washoe and Clark Counties have delayed proceedings.
Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democratic state senator and Lutheran minister, defeated Representative Zach Nunn, Republican of Iowa, according to The Associated Press, flipping a key seat to help her party win control of the House.
Ms. Trone Garriott’s victory over Mr. Nunn, a two-term incumbent who had closely aligned himself with President Trump, was a major breakthrough for Democrats in a district that Mr. Nunn had won twice. Republicans had invested millions of dollars there to defend one of their most vulnerable incumbents.
It was also a rebuke of the Trump administration’s economic agenda in a politically divided stretch of central and southern Iowa, where Ms. Trone Garriott had made rising costs, health care cuts and the economic consequences of the war in Iran central to her campaign.
Throughout the race, Ms. Trone Garriott sought to cast Mr. Nunn as a politician more concerned with protecting the president and his wealthy supporters than with the financial struggles of ordinary Iowans.
“Families are paying too much for groceries, health care and child care, and people are tired of politicians in Washington who look out for themselves,” she said last month, summarizing her central argument.
Her victory demonstrated the potency of that message in Iowa’s Third Congressional District, which encompasses Des Moines, its fast-growing suburbs and a broad swath of rural Iowa where Republicans have maintained considerable political strength.
A former Air Force intelligence officer, Mr. Nunn, 47, had spent much of his time in Congress as a steadfast supporter of Mr. Trump’s agenda. He repeatedly backed legislation that cut federal Medicaid spending, declined to break with the president over his sweeping tariffs and for months supported the war in Iran.
But as polling showed growing dissatisfaction with the war and its economic consequences, Mr. Nunn sought to distance himself from the administration. In September, after repeatedly rejecting efforts to restrict the president’s military authority, he joined a small group of Republicans who voted to curtail Mr. Trump’s ability to continue waging the war.
The shift was not enough to save him.
Ms. Trone Garriott, who had opposed the war, repeatedly tied the military operation to rising gasoline and fertilizer prices, arguing that Iowa families and farmers were paying the price for a conflict Congress had never authorized.
She also attacked Mr. Nunn’s support for the Republican domestic policy law that reduced Medicaid spending, accusing him of endangering access to health care in rural communities already struggling to keep hospitals and clinics open.
Ms. Trone Garriott, who defeated a powerful Republican incumbent to win her State Senate seat, held public town halls in all 21 counties of the congressional district, making her accessibility to constituents a central contrast with Mr. Nunn.
She also proved to be a formidable fund-raiser, bringing in more than $8 million by late October, substantially more than Mr. Nunn’s approximately $6 million. Outside Republican groups poured millions into defending his seat even as some of the party’s most powerful super PACs withdrew support from another vulnerable Iowa incumbent, Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks.
Mr. Nunn had demonstrated considerable political staying power, rooted in his popularity beyond the Democratic stronghold of Des Moines. But Ms. Trone Garriott appealed to suburban voters and sought to cut into the large margins Republicans traditionally enjoyed in rural communities.
Adam Hamilton’s victory in the Kansas Senate race represents a significant expansion of the Democrats’ footprint in the state. He carried 11 counties, winning back three that voted Democratic in the 2022 governor’s race but then flipped to Trump in 2024. He also flipped three counties that voted Republican in both 2022 and 2024.
In a victory speech, Josh Turek, Iowa’s Democratic senator-elect, cast his underdog win as proof of the power of the many over the concentrated wealth of the few. “We have proved that the impossible was possible,” he said, adding later, “We outvoted the billionaires.”
Grinning, he welcomed former Senator Tom Harkin, an Iowa Democrat, onto the stage and again credited him with paving the way for his political career as the author of the Americans With Disabilities Act. “I have been saying that it’s going to be beautifully poetic that the man that is coming to get Senator Harkin’s seat back is only there because of the work that he did.”
Turnout in Texas will end in the range of 10 million ballots cast, a record showing for a midterm election in the state that approaches turnout typically seen in a presidential race. It was strongest in areas that James Talarico won, particularly in majority-Hispanic counties like Cameron, Caldwell and Webb, which saw modest declines between 6 percent and 12 percent from two years ago. Midterm turnout often decreases much more sharply.
Richard Pan, a former Democratic state senator, defeated Representative Kevin Kiley, a Republican who changed his registration to independent this year, to win the House seat in a redrawn Northern California district, according to The Associated Press. Pan, a pediatrician who as a state lawmaker was known for passing bills to toughen school vaccine requirements, capitalized in a district where Democrats now outnumber Republicans, 3 to 1. Kiley, who has represented a rural stretch of Northern California in the House since 2022, tried to distance himself from President Trump’s policies.
Representative Max Miller, the Ohio Republican whose campaign was rocked by accusations that he physically abused his ex-wife and young daughter, lost his re-election bid, according to The Associated Press, handing Democrats a seat in deep-red territory as they won House control.
Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker, defeated Mr. Miller, a two-term congressman whose political rise was fueled by his close relationship with President Trump, in a district Mr. Trump won by a double-digit margin two years ago. Mr. Miller had rejected calls by fellow Republicans to drop out of the race after he was accused by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, of domestic abuse against her and their 2-year-old daughter.
Ms. Moreno, the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno, also an Ohio Republican, said that Mr. Miller had scalded her chest and stomach by throwing hot water from a skillet at her body; held a gun to her head; pushed her against a wall and hit her head; and fractured their daughter’s collarbone and bruised her shoulder. The allegations came to light as part of a lengthy divorce court battle.
Mr. Miller denied all of the accusations and embarked on a defiant media tour in which he accused his ex-wife of being mentally unstable, a liar, a stalker and a dangerous individual.
As the sordid family drama gained national attention, some powerful Ohio Republicans, including Senator Jon Husted, pressed Mr. Miller to exit the race and resign. Mr. Moreno, who at first tried to avoid questions about Mr. Miller, eventually said that his former son-in-law was not fit to hold public office.
“If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Mr. Moreno said in an emotional statement. The House Ethics Committee also opened a review of the domestic abuse allegations.
Some White House officials wanted Mr. Miller to drop out of the race in time for Republicans to replace him on the ballot, but the president stopped short of asking Mr. Miller to drop out.
In a private phone call, Mr. Trump simply warned him that it might be difficult for him to win given the allegations. Mr. Miller was resolute that he would do what the president himself had done when faced with personal scandals seen as fatal to his presidential campaigns: stay in and fight.
Mr. Poindexter continued to work full time as an apprentice instructor throughout his primary campaign. He tried to make his own relatable life story part of his pitch to win over working-class Trump voters.
“I never got in this race to run because Max Miller is terrible in his personal life,” he said in an interview. “I got in it to run because of policies that hurt us.”
Despite the accusations, Mr. Miller was never fully deserted by House Republican leaders. Once it became clear there was no way to replace him on the ballot, they quietly spent more than $5 million to defend his seat, according to the ad-tracking service AdImpact.
Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson won the race for governor in Michigan on Wednesday, according to The Associated Press, keeping in Democratic hands an office that has an important role in certifying the closely divided state’s presidential election results.
Ms. Benson, 49, will take over in January from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat who was barred by term limits from running again, and who built a national profile during eight years in Lansing. Ms. Benson defeated Representative John James, a Republican from suburban Detroit who had lost two previous statewide campaigns.
Both candidates made an anti-incumbent case to an electorate frustrated by the high cost of living and rising prices.
While Mr. James blamed the Democrats in state government, Ms. Benson criticized President Trump’s policies, including tariffs targeting Canada that have had an outsized effect on Michigan’s auto industry. She pledged to seek “sub-national” agreements with Canada, which borders Michigan, if elected.
“At a time where it feels like, at the federal level, government is showing up everywhere we don’t want it and nowhere where we actually need it, I will make sure that government is showing up for you and doing right by you,” Ms. Benson said in a recent debate hosted by WDIV-TV.
Ms. Benson, a former law school dean who served two terms as Michigan’s chief elections officer, became a target of right-wing activists in 2020 when she presided over Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory in the state over Mr. Trump. Ms. Benson defended the results against unproven claims of widespread fraud. After Mr. Trump returned to office, she fought his administration’s efforts to obtain private voter data.
Michigan’s governor signs a document certifying the state’s presidential electors, a role that could again become important if the results of a future presidential race are contested. Mr. Trump carried the state in 2016 and 2024, while Mr. Biden won it in 2020.
Ms. Benson will become the first Democratic governor of Michigan to succeed a fellow Democrat since the 1960s. She will also be the third woman to serve as the state’s leader.
The governor’s race had initially been expected to be a three-way contest including Mike Duggan, a former mayor of Detroit and longtime Democrat who was running as an independent. Though he received significant endorsements and had competitive polling numbers, Mr. Duggan dropped out of the race in May, saying he did not want to be a spoiler. His decision to withdraw was widely seen as a boost for Democrats.
Democrats won control of the House early Wednesday, capping a sweeping takeover of Congress as they harnessed a backlash against President Trump to end Republicans’ governing trifecta and secure a powerful foothold from which to check his power.
Capitalizing on widespread dissatisfaction over the war in Iran, Mr. Trump’s tariffs and corruption allegations, Democrats won decisive victories across the country, reaching deep into Republican territory where voters had soured on the president and his allies.
Having won control of the Senate despite a map stacked against them, Democrats early Wednesday clinched the 218 seats needed to take control of the House of Representatives, according to The Associated Press, and appeared on track to capture many more.
With final results still outstanding, it was unclear exactly how large Democrats’ majority would be, a factor that will shape their ability to set an agenda and muscle bills through the Senate, where Republicans retained the ability to block major measures from the minority.
But in a thrashing for the G.O.P., Democrats had won decisive victories across the country, including in solid conservative bastions, in what was projected early Wednesday morning to be the largest popular vote victory for either party since 1976.
The election results promised a new era of divided government in Washington and a freshly assertive Congress after two years in which Republicans generally ceded power to Mr. Trump and reduced the legislative branch’s role to that of a mere bystander. It capped a fiercely fought midterm election cycle that Democrats entered chastened from the 2024 presidential election but finished buoyant and with strong political winds at their backs.
“The American people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader who is now in line to be speaker, told supporters in Washington. “They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people.”
Senator Chuck Schumer, the New York Democrat and the longtime leader who was deeply involved in his party’s uphill battle for the majority, vowed a swift change in direction.
“We have five words for the American people,” he told reporters in Washington. “Relief is on the way.”
With control of Congress and its committees, Democrats are expected to deploy their oversight powers to aggressively investigate Mr. Trump and his administration over allegations of corruption, aggressive immigration enforcement tactics and the president’s pardons.
Representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is poised to be the chairman of the Oversight Committee, the main investigative panel in the House, issued a warning in a statement on Tuesday night.
“Lawyer up,” he said.
Democrats have also promised a shock-and-awe legislative sprint in which they plan to push through bills that would restore health care subsidies and Medicaid funding, address the increased costs of food and fuel and seek to force Mr. Trump to roll back his tariffs and end the war with Iran.
Democratic control of the Senate will also give the party veto power over Mr. Trump’s judicial and administration nominees, as well as the leadership of the committees that will have the authority to subpoena administration officials and others.
Mr. Trump, who appeared stunned by the results even as he deflected any blame for the losses, insisted he would still have the upper hand over a Democratic Congress.
“I have total veto power, so they have to come to us,” he said in an interview with The New York Times as the Democratic victories piled up. “And if they have some good ideas, I’m certainly open to working.”
Despite their losses in the last presidential election, Democrats had been consistently bullish about their ability to win the House majority. The party out of power typically gains seats in midterm elections, and Republicans have held only a slender majority in the House since they took over in 2023.
They were less optimistic about their prospects in the Senate, where the political map was stacked against them with seats in states that had become solidly Republican during the Trump era.
But as voters who backed Mr. Trump in 2024 began souring on the president and his agenda, Democrats saw an opportunity to drastically expand their political map. They won in longtime G.O.P. bastions like Kansas and Texas, reversed years of losses in Iowa and Ohio, and flipped both North Carolina and South Carolina.
Mr. Schumer recalled that when he first began talking about reclaiming the majority in 2025, “people rolled their eyes.” Democrats, he argued, prevailed because they heeded voters who were frustrated with how things were going in Washington and felt ignored by Republicans.
“We listened; they didn’t,” he said. “And the American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks.”
Their victories were powered by Americans’ growing dismay over the rising costs of goods and fuel linked to Mr. Trump’s tariffs and the war. Democrats painted the G.O.P. as beholden to the president and indifferent to the financial struggles of everyday Americans.
Those arguments were bolstered by growing concerns among voters about corruption in Washington and the cuts to Medicaid and health care subsidies that Republicans enacted as part of their signature tax cut and domestic policy package last year.
Their strength became evident early in the night, when Democrats surged in crucial House battlegrounds and had notched victories in competitive races in Florida, Pennsylvania and North Carolina. The party needed a net gain of only three seats to win the House.
Aware of the historical trend, Republicans had taken efforts to stem their expected losses with a frenzy of redistricting in red states that was meant to increase the number of G.O.P.-leaning districts and force Democrats out of what had been safe seats.
But those moves fell short in the face of Mr. Trump’s plummeting approval ratings. In Florida, Democrats won in three districts that Republican state lawmakers redrew to favor their party, including some where Mr. Trump won by more than 10 percentage points in 2024.
Even with many races uncalled, Speaker Mike Johnson effectively acknowledged his party’s defeat on Tuesday night.
“We knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority, we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history,” Mr. Johnson said. “It’s very, very difficult to overcome. And it looks like history will be kept tonight.”
The drubbing appeared to leave many Republicans reeling on Tuesday evening, and raised questions about the direction that the party would take in the final two years of Mr. Trump’s second term, a lame-duck period that has bedeviled many presidents.
Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the Republican leader, said his party would work to thwart Democrats at every turn.
“As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done,” Mr. Thune said in a statement early Wednesday. “Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we’ll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism. We cannot let their fringe positions become the mainstream.”
During the first half of his second term, Mr. Trump has enjoyed near-total control of Congress, with lawmakers showing little appetite for imposing guardrails on his actions.
But Senate races in particular suggested that Mr. Trump had lost his once dominant sway over Republican voters. The president won both North Carolina and South Carolina in all three of his presidential elections. But in both cases in this election, his handpicked candidates trailed significantly.
And with Mr. Trump losing ground even in Ohio and Iowa, two former battleground states that he transformed into G.O.P. strongholds, it was unclear whether he would exhibit the same hold on Republican lawmakers that has characterized his second term.
Sensing a political shift in the final weeks of their campaigns, many vulnerable lawmakers sought to put some distance between themselves and his policies, particularly his signature tariffs. But the pivot appeared to have come too late.
Annie Karni and Robert Jimison contributed reporting from Washington.

Most US election seats are reliably won by one party, so control of Congress comes down to a few competitive "battleground" seats. Experts track these to predict overall results; if a party wins seats they were expected to lose, it often signals a successful night. House results

Governor results
Gubernatorial elections were taking place in 36 states, as well as three territories. Republicans and Democrats held 18 of these state governorships each before the election. Three incumbent governors were retiring.
Election explained
Election explained
How the elections work
The US legislature, Congress, has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate.
How is the House of Representatives elected and how do they work?
The lower chamber, the House of Representatives, has 435 voting seats, each representing a district of roughly similar size. There are elections for each of these seats every two years.
The speaker of the House is the chamber’s presiding officer, elected by the representatives. The House has several exclusive powers, such as the power to initiate revenue bills, impeach federal officials and elect the president in the case of an electoral college tie.
How is the Senate elected and how do they work?
The upper chamber, the Senate, has 100 members, who sit for six-year terms. One-third of the seats come up for election in each two-year cycle. Each state has two senators, regardless of its population; this means that Wyoming, with a population of less than 600,000, carries the same weight as California, with almost 40 million.
Most legislation needs to pass both chambers to become law, but the Senate has some important other functions, notably approving senior presidential appointments, for instance to the supreme court. The Senate also has the sole power to provide advice to the president, consent to ratify treaties and try impeachment cases for federal officials referred to it by the House.
In most states, the candidate with the most votes on election day wins the seat. However, Georgia and Louisiana require the winning candidate to garner 50% of votes cast; if no one does, they hold a runoff election between the top two candidates.
Maine and Alaska use ranked-choice voting as opposed to the first past the post voting system in congressional elections. Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the least-supported candidate is eliminated and their ballots are transferred to each voter’s next-ranked candidate. This continues until a candidate wins a majority.
In some states, an election can feature two candidates from the same party. Under top-two or “jungle” primary systems, candidates from all parties compete in the same primary and the two receiving the most votes advance, regardless of party. The congressional election candidates could both be Democrats or both be Republicans.
Florida and Ohio are having ‘special elections’ for the Senate because the previous holders of their seats – Marco Rubio and JD Vance – resigned to join the executive branch following the 2024 presidential election.
How are governors elected and how do they work?
Governors are elected by direct vote in their states. The candidate with the highest number of votes is declared the winner.
In every state, the executive branch is led by a governor. They serve for four years in office, with the exception of Vermont and New Hampshire where tenures are two years long.
Governors are responsible for implementing state laws, and have a range of powers available to them such as executive orders, executive budgets and legislative proposals and vetoes.
How are the results reported?
The election results on this page are reported by the Associated Press. AP will “call” the winner in a state when it determines that the trailing candidate has no path to victory. This can happen before 100% of votes in a state have been counted.
Estimates for the total vote in each state are also provided by AP. The numbers update throughout election night and in the following days, as more data on voter turnout becomes available.
Antonio Voce, Seán Clarke, Ed Gargan, Anna Leach and Ashley Kirk

AI stocks slide as Texas governor result raises data center risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
07:00:20 UTC
16:00:20 KST

Shares of Elon Musk's SpaceX and Tesla fell in premarket trading Wednesday as the Democrats won a significant victory in the midterm elections.
SpaceX was last trading down 4.6% and Tesla dropped 4.4% amid big losses for Republican candidates Musk had backed.
Artificial intelligence stocks came under pressure overnight as Democrats — seen as proponents of data center moratoriums — won big in midterm elections in key data center hubs.
The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk, where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats.
SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas.
The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning.
"There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said.
He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet.
Mixed moves for AI stocks
The more direct plays were mixed. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 0.8% and 1.9%, respectively. Peer Nebius Group was up 2.9% and Oracle shed 1.3%.
Tech giants Nvidia, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft were all up around 1-2%, with Amazon rising 2.7%. AMD shares rose 6.3% after announcing earnings on Tuesday.
Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 were up 1%. The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) was up 1.5%.
Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow. Democrat Gina Hinojosa is the projected winner over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, according to the Associated Press.
"The one thing that could really end up moving stuff though would be if Abbott were to lose Texas," said Scott Ladner, chief investment officer of Horizon Investments, earlier Tuesday as results rolled in. "Because there is a legitimate question about where do you build these data centers?"
"Texas is a fertile ground for that. And if he were to lose, I think that fertile ground is largely barren. So, that's going to be a challenge," Ladner added.
Hinojosa has been outspoken in her support of a moratorium on AI data centers. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State.
'Left-tail event'
The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing.
"We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week.
Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo.
Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end.
"Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

US midterm elections 2026 live updates: Democrats win Senate control and edge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
06:00:30 UTC
15:00:30 KST

The Democratic party has taken control of Congress in a major setback for Donald Trump and Republicans. Here are some of the key results, historic victories and political developments from the midterm elections so far:
The Democrats have secured 228 seats in the House (with 218 needed for a majority) and 54 seats in the Senate (with 51 needed for control). The party has flipped at least seven Senate seats in red states and battlegrounds, including Kansas – which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century – Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. In the House, the Democrats have flipped more than two dozen districts.
History was made in Michigan as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Republican Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat. “You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed said in his election night speech.
Other seismic wins in federal and state races for the Democrats include James Talarico, who became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton, who is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; and progressive Troy Jackson, who unseated Susan Collins in Maine, ending her 30-year career in the US Senate.
Democrat Aaron Ford won the race for governor in Nevada, toppling Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and becoming the state’s first black governor.
Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”
Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics. “Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face,” he said.
Fox News host Sean Hannity, one of Donald Trump’s most prominent supporters in conservative media, has acknowledged that the scale of public “hatred” towards the US president contributed to the Republicans’ heavy midtern election losses.
“Hatred is a hell of a motivator,” he told fellow panellist Harold Ford Jr.
He added: “I think the hatred for this man is unprecedented. I’ve never seen anything like it.”
In another historic first, the Democrats are projected to win Nevada’s second congressional district for the first time since its creation in 1981.
Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson is in the lead ahead of Republican David Flippo, although the race has not yet been called by the Associated Press.
If she holds on to that lead and flips the House seat, it will mark the first time since 1947 that Nevada has had an all-Democrat congressional delegation. Democrat incumbents have swept all of Nevada’s three remaining House seats, whose races have been called by AP.
“One of the biggest upsets in Nevada history, a district never held by a Democrat in its 45 years of existence,” said Jon Ralston, founder and CEO of the Nevada Independent, of Benitez-Thompson’s projected win.
Democrat James Talarico has won the US Senate race in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold and delivering a stunning blow to Donald Trump.
Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and a staunch ally of the US president, in one of the most closely watched contests of the midterm elections to decide control of Congress.
“We just took back Texas!” the 37-year-old told jubilant supporters at an election night party in Austin, the state capital and his home city. “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We have just shown that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love.”
Democrat Aaron Ford makes history as Nevada elects its first black governor
Nevada has elected Democrat Aaron Ford as its next governor, making him the first black person to hold the office in the state’s history.
His win toppled the Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo in a closely watched race, and delivered an important victory for the Democrats in one of the country’s key battleground states.
Ford ran his campaign with the backing of California governor Gavin Newsom and former vice-president Kamala Harris, focusing on the cost of living, housing affordability and student debt.
Opinion: The death knell of Trumpism has finally sounded
Moira Donegan
There’s a certain freedom in low expectations. Going in to Tuesday’s midterm elections, forecasts were so grim for the Republicans that poll watchers started trading a kind of knowing joke: that the results would either mean the end of the Trump era, or the end of the polling profession.
Amid those sorts of predictions, any Republican victories would have seemed like a minor miracle. The expectation was that Democrats would have a blowout; Republicans, counting on the final tally to be a bit more mixed, would therefore almost certainly have the freedom to claim that they’d done better than anyone had thought they would.
It will be difficult to credit those spins today. The electorate issued the president a message of dissatisfaction with the second Trump term, and voted decisively to curb his power.
Now, with a Senate majority, Democrats will be able to investigate the president and his cabinet members, draw public attention to their own agenda items, assert Congress’s constitutional prerogatives, and block Republican judicial appointments.
In the coming days and weeks, Trump will alternately say that the Republican losses were fake – the result of fraud by a nefarious but ill-defined conspiracy of Democrats and illegal immigrants – and that they were real, but somebody else’s fault.
His administration has signaled over the past weeks that it could make efforts to contest the certification of especially close Senate races, notably Alaska.
But the wind may have gone out of the sails of that plan for now: for what it’s worth, which isn’t much, Trump told the New York Times on Tuesday night that he would accept the results of the midterms. What’s certain is that he will rail into microphones and complain in all caps on social media. But it is not likely that any of that will go anywhere. Because Tuesday night – almost exactly 10 years after he won the presidency in an upset victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016 – the Trump era effectively came to an end.
'The American people sent a clear message,' says Obama
Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics.
In a statement on X, he said:
Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face.
These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country – including in areas once considered long shots. They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first.”
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.
“Yesterday, the American people voted against policies that only serve to impoverish people,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”
Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added: “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”
Republican Pete Ricketts wins re-election in Nebraska Senate race
Republican senator Pete Ricketts has won his re-election bid in Nebraska, defeating independent candidate Dan Osborn.
Ricketts, a former Nebraska governor, was appointed to the Senate in 2023 to replace Republican senator Ben Sasse and won a special election in 2024 to serve the final two years of his predecessor’s term.
History was made in Michigan as Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat.
His victory is all the more remarkable given the ugly campaign of anti-Muslim rhetoric that sought to undermine his candidacy, led by Donald Trump and his Republican allies.
In his victory speech, El-Sayed told a jubilant crowd:
My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honoured to stand here as your Senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.
Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into an alhamdulillah (praise be to God).”
It’s 3am ET in Washington/8am GMT, and as people start seeing their phones ping with notifications, here are where things stand at the moment.
Democrats have won control of Congress in a stunning rebuke of Donald Trump’s agenda, delivering an astonishing result and a widely predicted “blue wave” across the country. As of now, Democrats have clinched 54 seats in the Senate (they needed 51 to reclaim the majority) and 225 House seats (they needed 218 to take control of the lower chamber). We’re still awaiting the results for several races – namely in Alaska.
There were several seismic and historic wins in federal and state races for Democrats. James Talarico became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; In Maine, progressive Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins after a thirty-year grip on the state’s US Senate seat; and Abdul El-Sayed won the US senate race in Michigan – one of the cycle’s most closely watched competitions.
We’re waiting on a number of nail-biting races to be called. The race for US Senate in Mississippi is extremely close, and could see a Democratic upset, and it’s still to early to call the Senate contest in Alaska.
Democrats also made history in a number of gubernatorial races.Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia means that she will be the first Black female governor in US history. Gina Hinojosa makes history as Texas’ first Latina governor, and the first Democrat to occupy the governor’s mansion since 1990. Meanwhile, David Crowley became Wisconsin’s first Black governor after winning his race tonight.
Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”

US midterm elections 2026 live updates: Democrats win Senate control and edge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
06:00:30 UTC
15:00:30 KST

The Democratic party has taken control of Congress in a major setback for Donald Trump and Republicans. Here are some of the key results, historic victories and political developments from the midterm elections so far:
The Democrats have secured 228 seats in the House (with 218 needed for a majority) and 54 seats in the Senate (with 51 needed for control). The party has flipped at least seven Senate seats in red states and battlegrounds, including Kansas – which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century – Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. In the House, the Democrats have flipped more than two dozen districts.
History was made in Michigan as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Republican Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat. “You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed said in his election night speech.
Other seismic wins in federal and state races for the Democrats include James Talarico, who became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton, who is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; and progressive Troy Jackson, who unseated Susan Collins in Maine, ending her 30-year career in the US Senate.
Democrat Aaron Ford won the race for governor in Nevada, toppling Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and becoming the state’s first black governor.
Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”
Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics. “Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face,” he said.
Fox News host Sean Hannity, one of Donald Trump’s most prominent supporters in conservative media, has acknowledged that the scale of public “hatred” towards the US president contributed to the Republicans’ heavy midtern election losses.
“Hatred is a hell of a motivator,” he told fellow panellist Harold Ford Jr.
He added: “I think the hatred for this man is unprecedented. I’ve never seen anything like it.”
In another historic first, the Democrats are projected to win Nevada’s second congressional district for the first time since its creation in 1981.
Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson is in the lead ahead of Republican David Flippo, although the race has not yet been called by the Associated Press.
If she holds on to that lead and flips the House seat, it will mark the first time since 1947 that Nevada has had an all-Democrat congressional delegation. Democrat incumbents have swept all of Nevada’s three remaining House seats, whose races have been called by AP.
“One of the biggest upsets in Nevada history, a district never held by a Democrat in its 45 years of existence,” said Jon Ralston, founder and CEO of the Nevada Independent, of Benitez-Thompson’s projected win.
Democrat James Talarico has won the US Senate race in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold and delivering a stunning blow to Donald Trump.
Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and a staunch ally of the US president, in one of the most closely watched contests of the midterm elections to decide control of Congress.
“We just took back Texas!” the 37-year-old told jubilant supporters at an election night party in Austin, the state capital and his home city. “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We have just shown that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love.”
Democrat Aaron Ford makes history as Nevada elects its first black governor
Nevada has elected Democrat Aaron Ford as its next governor, making him the first black person to hold the office in the state’s history.
His win toppled the Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo in a closely watched race, and delivered an important victory for the Democrats in one of the country’s key battleground states.
Ford ran his campaign with the backing of California governor Gavin Newsom and former vice-president Kamala Harris, focusing on the cost of living, housing affordability and student debt.
Opinion: The death knell of Trumpism has finally sounded
Moira Donegan
There’s a certain freedom in low expectations. Going in to Tuesday’s midterm elections, forecasts were so grim for the Republicans that poll watchers started trading a kind of knowing joke: that the results would either mean the end of the Trump era, or the end of the polling profession.
Amid those sorts of predictions, any Republican victories would have seemed like a minor miracle. The expectation was that Democrats would have a blowout; Republicans, counting on the final tally to be a bit more mixed, would therefore almost certainly have the freedom to claim that they’d done better than anyone had thought they would.
It will be difficult to credit those spins today. The electorate issued the president a message of dissatisfaction with the second Trump term, and voted decisively to curb his power.
Now, with a Senate majority, Democrats will be able to investigate the president and his cabinet members, draw public attention to their own agenda items, assert Congress’s constitutional prerogatives, and block Republican judicial appointments.
In the coming days and weeks, Trump will alternately say that the Republican losses were fake – the result of fraud by a nefarious but ill-defined conspiracy of Democrats and illegal immigrants – and that they were real, but somebody else’s fault.
His administration has signaled over the past weeks that it could make efforts to contest the certification of especially close Senate races, notably Alaska.
But the wind may have gone out of the sails of that plan for now: for what it’s worth, which isn’t much, Trump told the New York Times on Tuesday night that he would accept the results of the midterms. What’s certain is that he will rail into microphones and complain in all caps on social media. But it is not likely that any of that will go anywhere. Because Tuesday night – almost exactly 10 years after he won the presidency in an upset victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016 – the Trump era effectively came to an end.
'The American people sent a clear message,' says Obama
Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics.
In a statement on X, he said:
Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face.
These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country – including in areas once considered long shots. They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first.”
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.
“Yesterday, the American people voted against policies that only serve to impoverish people,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”
Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added: “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”
Republican Pete Ricketts wins re-election in Nebraska Senate race
Republican senator Pete Ricketts has won his re-election bid in Nebraska, defeating independent candidate Dan Osborn.
Ricketts, a former Nebraska governor, was appointed to the Senate in 2023 to replace Republican senator Ben Sasse and won a special election in 2024 to serve the final two years of his predecessor’s term.
History was made in Michigan as Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat.
His victory is all the more remarkable given the ugly campaign of anti-Muslim rhetoric that sought to undermine his candidacy, led by Donald Trump and his Republican allies.
In his victory speech, El-Sayed told a jubilant crowd:
My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honoured to stand here as your Senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.
Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into an alhamdulillah (praise be to God).”

India’s EloElo nabs $80M from NBCUniversal to bet on the country’s rising microdrama market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
04:45:00 UTC
13:45:00 KST

More than 118 million users watch microdramas every month as the serialized format has taken off in India. EloElo’s Story TV is one of the top apps for microdramas, with over 33 million active users, according to analysts.
Banking on that scale, the company has raised $80 million in Series C from Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal. This round brings its total fundraising to $130 million, with a valuation of $500 million.
As people spend more time on platforms hosting verticalized videos, serialized content has become popular in multiple geographies, including the U.S., China, and India, with Hollywood celebrities like Issa Rae, James Franco, and Kim Kardashian investing in and starring in the format.
Given India’s massive internet population of more than a billion and the country’s appetite for entertainment content, it presents a big market opportunity, with analysts expecting the industry to cross $3-$4 billion in annual revenue by 2030. Last year, dedicated apps like Story TV, Kuku TV, and Quick TV were among the top downloaded video streaming apps in the country.
Founded in 2020 by former Flipkart exec Saurabh Pandey, the Story TV platform has taken off in the last few years with a catalog of over 5,000 titles in six languages. Pandey told TechCrunch that because of the snackable content format, users log 95 minutes on the app on average through multiple sessions in a day.
“I fundamentally believe that the next billion users will probably not grow up on a diet of watching television; they will grow up on a diet of watching content on their phones, right? And this content has to be, and this entertainment, designed very differently. It’s not going to be appointment viewing. It’s going to be within certain slots throughout the day. And a lot of this was earlier solved for short clips, but serialized storytelling was never solved,” Pandey said about the microdrama format.
He believes that there still will be a place for big-screen viewing with family or friends, but the majority of entertainment consumption would be done through mobile.
All microdrama platforms compete against platforms like YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok, where creators are posting content for free. Some of them are also creating a way for creators to post serialized content. Pandey thinks that producing quality content on the platform will entice users to choose StoryTV over other free platforms. The company points to its partnerships, such as the one with Indian TV production company Balaji Telefilms, to produce content.
The company offers different kinds of subscriptions ranging from monthly, quarterly, and yearly to unlock content. It also offers some free content supported by ads, which might not be as lucrative a medium to make money as subscriptions, according to reports.
Monetization is a challenge in India, as users often stick around for free content, but few convert to paid users. A report from analyst firm Redseer indicates that more than 40 million people have paid for microdrama at least once, but only 15-17 million users pay for it on a monthly basis. A separate survey by Ormax Media suggested that 72% of people haven’t ever paid while consuming microdrama.
AI and other bets
All microdrama platforms want to have enough supply to engage different audiences and want to involve AI to solve that. Some platforms, like Google-backed Kuku, want to improve workflows and create more content, and some platforms like Dashverse’s Shortfree want to use video AI models to create serialized clips.
At the moment, StoryTV falls into the first camp with its Dolphin AI platform. Started as an internal tool to improve video creation, the company is now planning to make the tool widely available. It can act as an editor with templates and an array of models to create images, audio, and video, according to its website.
EloElo’s vision is to have people use this tool for marketing campaigns and ads as well. Notably, while Indian platforms like Pocket and Kuku have built AI tools and given them to creators, it is likely to accelerate their content pipeline. But at InVideo, there hasn’t been a scaled effort to provide a good alternative to CapCut or Instagram Edits to creators from India.
Pandey believes that human involvement is still paramount to producing good stories, and AI tools are still creative directors for steering.
“My belief in involving AI is that AI is a really fast race car where AI is the engine, but you need an extremely capable Formula One driver to be on the steering wheel. That, for me, is the creative director or the showrunner. AI is supposed to work with them, augmenting their skill set. AI can help write stories, but so far the best stories I have loved have all had a very high human x AI element to it,” he said.
Besides microdrama, the company also has a vertical video learning app, Master, competing with the likes of Seekho and Kuku’s Guru, and an AI companion app, Voxy AI. The company said that it has more than 40 million monthly users across its apps. While it didn’t bifurcate users by app, the majority of users belong to Story TV.
EloElo currently has 240 people and wants to hire to increase the size of its AI and machine learning research team. The company is also deploying a good chunk of its capital to produce more original titles.
MIT Investment Co., along with existing investors like Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures, and Griffin Gaming Partners, invested in the round.

Democrats win control of the House of Representatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
03:36:23 UTC
12:36:23 KST

Democrats won control of the House of Representatives with what could be their largest majority in nearly two decades, NBC News projects, as voters delivered a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump and Republicans.
The House projection is based on an analysis that Democrats will win about 255 House seats — an estimate that could still tick up or down by a few seats but will be well beyond the 218 needed to secure a majority.
NBC News has projected the Democrats will also flip control of the Senate, putting them in charge of both chambers.
Democrats needed to win a net of just three seats to take back the majority. The blue wave washed over many more GOP-held seats than that — from the East Coast to Texas’ Rio Grande Valley — most in districts that Trump carried in 2024.
A quartet of GOP incumbents in Pennsylvania were defeated. Democrat Bob Harvie beat GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a leader of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus; Democrat Bob Brooks knocked off GOP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th Congressional District; Paige Cognetti bested GOP Rep. Rob Bresnahan in the 8th District; and Democrat Janelle Stelson ousted GOP Rep. Scott Perry, a former chairman of the far-right Freedom Caucus, in the 10th District.
In Virginia, Democratic former Rep. Elaine Luria won back her old seat, defeating Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans in the Virginia Beach area, while Democrat Shannon Taylor upset longtime GOP Rep. Rob Wittman outside Richmond.
Another big name in Republican politics, Rep. Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey, lost his race for re-election to Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind., the first Ukrainian-born member of Congress, who frequently clashed with Trump and GOP leaders, also was defeated. And in Colorado, Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel trounced GOP Rep. Gabe Evans.
One of the biggest prizes of the night for Democrats was Richard Ojeda II’s upset of Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C. As chairman of the House GOP’s campaign arm, Hudson was responsible for protecting GOP incumbents and the majority.
The Democrats’ victory was widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s unpopular policies, including his tough immigration crackdown, the eight-month Iran war and tariffs on U.S. allies that drove up the prices of gas, groceries and other goods.
When the party takes control of the chamber on Jan. 3, it will be the first time in Trump’s second term that he won’t have full control of Congress.
Since he returned to the White House, Trump has tested the limits of his executive powers, dismantling federal agencies through the Department of Government Efficiency, unilaterally imposing sweeping tariffs and rescinding congressionally approved funding — all while the GOP-controlled House and Senate mostly looked the other way.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections
The House Democratic leader, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who barnstormed across the country in the final weeks of the campaign, is expected to make history on Jan. 3 when he is sworn in as the first Black speaker of the House.
He walked into his election night watch party to raucous cheers as the rap song “Unbelievable,” by the Notorious B.I.G., played on the speakers. The midterm results show the “American people are crying out for transformational change,” Jeffries told supporters.
“Today begins the great American comeback. The American people have spoken all across the land, in the North, in the South, in the East, in the West, in the Midwest, from sea to shining sea. The American people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,” Jeffries said at the gathering in Washington.
“They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people,” he said, “and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January.”
With their new majority, Democrats will take control of House committees, gaining subpoena power and the ability to conduct oversight investigations of Trump’s administration, family and business ventures. That could take up considerable time and resources for Trump and his allies, forcing uncomfortable public hearings or prompting legal showdowns over subpoenas.
And in a callback to Trump’s first term, some Democrats have vowed to impeach him for a third time, though there is an internal debate about whether that’s the right political path.
Jeffries told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out” on impeachment.
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., now poised to become chairman of the powerful Oversight Committee in January, said his panel plans to focus on “Trump family corruption,” including Trump’s cryptocurrency ventures, which have earned him more than $1 billion. The panel will also scrutinize “abuses” by ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, corporate corruption and the Jeffrey Epstein files.
Aside from investigative power, House Democrats will also command the ability to pass legislation with a simple majority. Jeffries has said Democrats would focus on four areas: reversing Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, extending the Affordable Care Act credits, restoring congressional authority related to tariffs and stopping Trump’s war with Iran.
“I wouldn’t characterize it as investigating them like crazy. We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries told reporters at Democrats’ campaign headquarters before the election.
The results are a blow to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who was launched from obscurity into the top job and has led House Republicans for the past three years. It’s unclear whether Johnson, a close Trump ally, will fight to remain as minority leader or step aside; the latter would trigger a fiercely competitive GOP race to replace him.
House Democrats had the political wind at their backs; they needed to flip a net of just three seats to win back the majority they lost in 2022. And Trump’s dismal approval rating was a major factor in the GOP’s loss.
Historically, the president’s party tends to lose seats in midterm elections. Only in two midterms in the modern era did a party buck that trend — in 1998, when voters punished Republicans for impeaching President Bill Clinton, and in 2002, as President George W. Bush rallied support in the wake of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.
Still, the battle for House control played out primarily on GOP turf this cycle, with Democrats already holding 215 seats, including a dozen in battleground districts. On top of that, results of this cycle’s mid-decade redistricting wars ended up favoring Republicans slightly, though Democrats quickly moved to neutralize what could have been a large GOP advantage.
Trump fired the first shot in the summer of 2025, when he urged GOP allies in Texas to redraw their congressional lines to help the party pick up as many as five seats. Republicans also redrew maps in places like Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, Alabama, Louisiana and Missouri in a bid to win more seats.
But Democrats countered in California, with Gov. Gavin Newsom, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and their allies successfully rallying support for Proposition 50, which approved a new congressional map drawn by state Democrats. That map helped Democrats pick up GOP-held seats.
While the GOP successfully picked up a handful of majority-Black, Democratic-held seats in the South, the Supreme Court blocked Missouri Republicans’ new congressional map, essentially preserving the Kansas City seat of longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.
“We made a promise to aggressively push back against the MAGA extremist effort to rip the election away from the American people by gerrymandering the possibility of Democrats winning the majority out of existence,” Jeffries said before the election, adding that the redistricting wars will continue in the 120th Congress.
“This fight is not over; we’ve just gotten started,” he added. “It will continue into the next Congress until we pass legislation signed into law by a future president that will prohibit mid-decade gerrymandering from ever happening again.”

Ukraine's Drone Strikes Spur Hasty Russian Plans For Underground Data Centers
