Ukraine's Drone Strikes Spur Hasty Russian Plans For Underground Data Centers (arstechnica.com) 24
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: [S]tate-owned telecommunications company Rostelcom has raised the possibility of moving some Russian data centers underground in talks with the nickel and palladium mining company Norilsk, according to Russian newspaper Vedomosti. The industry publication Data Center Dynamics also pointed to a recent proposal by a Russian regional governor to build data centers within open-pit coal mines while planting green public parks above as camouflage.
On November 2, Putin also signed a decree ordering Russian data center operators to set aside 10 percent of available space and capacity in case the Russian government requires it, according to independent Russian news publication Meduza. That may indicate growing Kremlin concerns about the vulnerability of Russian cloud computing infrastructure during its war with Ukraine. Putin's decree also allows a special Russian government commission to authorize use of foreign data centers in consultation with Russia's Federal Security Service. That marks a notable policy change because Putin and the Russian parliament previously enacted Russia's "Sovereign Internet Law," which has blocked Russian companies from using cloud computing infrastructure outside Russia's borders.
Russia's push for a sovereign and increasingly closed Internet has resulted in a highly centralized system under a few Russian tech companies like Yandex. That hyper-centralized system has now proven vulnerable during wartime, as Ukrainian drone strikes on key Russian data centers created widespread disruptions for popular payment and digital banking apps, e-commerce platforms, video streaming services, and ride-hailing and food delivery apps, among others. Yandex has also been forced to relocate all three of its main supercomputers after Ukrainian drone strikes targeted the AI data centers where they were originally housed, Meduza reported.

Distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in young patients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
03:20:13 UTC
12:20:13 KST

Study reveals distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in younger patients
Researchers identified age-associated differences in tumor composition and gene activity, creating a foundation for investigating why colorectal cancer can be more aggressive in younger adults
Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers, along with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation, and the Broad Institute, have uncovered biological clues to why colorectal cancer can behave more aggressively in younger people. Published today in Nature Medicine, the study — the largest of its kind — lays a foundation for understanding age-associated differences in colorectal cancer and exploring future treatments.
In the United States, colorectal cancer diagnosis rates among people younger than 50 rose 2.9% per year from 2013 through 2022, according to the American Cancer Society. Its 2026 report identifies colorectal cancer as the leading cause of cancer death in this age group. Younger patients are also more likely to be diagnosed at advanced stages, underscoring the need to better understand the biology of early-onset disease.
"Through Dana-Farber’s Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, we see how profoundly this disease can affect younger patients and their families, often during the busiest and most formative years of life," said co-senior author Kimmie Ng, MD, MPH, who is the director of the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber. "This collaborative work with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute and researchers from the Broad Institute gives us important new insight into the biology of these tumors. The findings provide a valuable roadmap for further investigating the distinct features of young-onset colorectal cancer. Our ultimate goal is to discover novel strategies for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment for our young patients."
"The need to understand why colorectal cancer is affecting younger adults at increasing rates is urgent," said co-senior author Ana C. Anderson, PhD, a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital, and Harvard Medical School. "And that starts with understanding the biology of the disease across the entire lifespan. By looking beyond conventional age cutoffs, we’ve uncovered biological patterns that earlier studies may have missed and created a foundation for the field to investigate them further. While we’re still at the beginning of understanding what these differences mean, our work gives researchers a new direction to pursue in tackling this urgent problem in human disease."
The research team, led by first author Caroline Porter, PhD, of the Klarman Cell Observatory at the Broad Institute, studied specimens from surgeries stored in Dana-Farber’s Gastrointestinal Biobank from surgeries at Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Co-senior authors include Anderson, Ng, and Ramnik J. Xavier, MD, PhD, of the Broad Institute, Mass General Brigham, and the Gene Lay Institute. They analyzed 189 tumors from patients ages 29 to 90+, including 54 diagnosed before age 50, and 135 diagnosed at age 50 or older. Using a technique called single-nucleus RNA sequencing, the researchers measured gene activity in more than 850,000 cancer cells and other cells in the tumors. The technique, which works with frozen tissue, enabled the team to build a detailed map of tumor cells by studying archived samples with extensive clinical record data.
Rather than dividing the tumor samples into two data sets and comparing the younger and older age groups, the researchers looked for factors that changed gradually with age, accounting for tumor location, stage, sex, and prior treatment in their analyses. This approach revealed subtle differences that likely would have been obscured by a simple two-data set comparison.
Among tumors of the most common colorectal cancer subtype, younger patients’ tumors had a significantly higher proportion of connective and supporting cells relative to cancer cells. A higher proportion of connective and supporting cells has been linked to chemotherapy resistance in several types of solid cancer. The team confirmed this pattern using gene-activity data from 564 other tumors and computer analysis of stained tissue images from another 712 tumors.
Younger patients also had higher activity of long non-coding RNAs, molecules that can regulate genes without making proteins. Some appeared repeatedly across different types of cancer cells. Many are "dark" RNAs, whose functions remain largely unknown. The team also saw gene activity suggesting stronger signaling between cells that can help cancer cells move and invade nearby tissue in younger patients.
"Our study is an advance from previous work in that we analyzed tumors from a large number of patients and used single-cell approaches to find novel features unique to tumors from young patients," said Xavier, a co-senior author of the study, a core institute member at the Broad Institute, Kurt Isselbacher Professor at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, and Vice Director of the Gene Lay Institute. Xavier is also a gastroenterologist at Mass General Brigham. "This work sets the stage for future mechanistic studies on how these cell programs interact with chemicals from the diet and from gut microbes to cause early-onset colorectal cancer."
Although the findings provide key insight into colorectal cancer in young individuals, they do not yet provide proof that these differences cause more aggressive disease. One remaining question is whether there are differences in immune responses in these tumors across ages — the researchers' methods captured relatively few immune cells. Future studies will explore how these changes may affect cancer growth and spread, and whether they offer opportunities for prevention or treatment.
Authorship: Authors include Caroline B. M. Porter, Shane P. Murphy, Jules Cazaubiel, Toni M. Delorey, Liat Amir-Zilberstein, Orr Ashenberg, Liubou Klindziuk, Elizabeth Andrews, William Tan, Kosuke Matsuda, Atsushi Kondo, Satoko Ugai, Tomotaka Ugai, Shuji Ogino, Emily Finan, Jacques Deguine, Ewa Sicinska, Lauren K. Brais, Jennifer S. Thalappillil, Marios Giannakis, Ramnik J. Xavier, Ana C. Anderson and Kimmie Ng.
Disclosures: Anderson is a member of the scientific advisory boards for Compass Therapeutics, Zumutor Biologics and Cytospire; these interests were reviewed and managed by Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Mass General Brigham in accordance with their conflict-of-interest policies. Ogino has served as a consultant for Sanofi Pasteur. Xavier is a co-founder of Convergence Bio, a scientific advisory board member at Nestlé and Magnet BioMedicine, and a board director at MoonLake Immunotherapeutics; these organizations had no role in the study. Deguine is a member of BioRender’s scientific advisory board. Giannakis receives institutional research funding from Janssen and Sunbird Bio, has consulted for Nerviano Medical Sciences, and has received honoraria from OncLive and PER. Ng consults for or serves on advisory boards for Bayer, Pfizer, CytomX, Jazz Pharmaceuticals, Revolution Medicines, Agenus, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, Sanofi, GlaxoSmithKline, Flagship Pioneering, AstraZeneca, Amgen, CRICO and Manta Cares; receives institutional research funding from Pharmavite and Janssen; and serves as an Associate Editor at JAMA. Her interests were reviewed and managed by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in accordance with its conflict-of-interest policies.
Funding: This study was funded in part by the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation, Helen Gurley Brown Foundation/Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Project P Fund, Patrick Beauregard Fund, Poorvu-Jaffe Fund for Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Research, The Thau Fund, the Eigner Fund for Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer, the Klarman Cell Observatory at Broad Institute, National Institutes of Health (R01 CA205406, P30 DK043351, R01 CA285851, P01 CA87969, UM1 CA186107, P01 CA55075, UM1 CA167552, U01 CA167552, R01 CA151993, R35 CA197735), and the American Cancer Society Clinical Research Professor Award (CRP-24-1185864-01-PROF).

Arrows to arrows, categories to queries (2025)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
03:11:27 UTC
12:11:27 KST

Arrows to Arrows, Categories to Queries
I’ve had a little time off of work as of late, and been spending it in characteristically unwise ways. In particular, I’ve written a little programming language that compiles to SQL. I call it catlang. That’s not to say that I’ve written a new query language. It’s a programming language, whose compiler spits out one giant SELECT statement. When you run that query in postgres, you get the output of your program.
Why have I done this? Because I needed a funny compilation target to test out the actual features of the language, which is that its intermediary language is a bunch of abstract category theory nonsense. Which I’ll get to. But I’m sure you first want to see this bad boy in action.
Behold, the function that returns 100 regardless of what input you give it. But it does it with the equivalent of a while loop:
count : Int -> Int
count =
  x ->
    loop x
      i ->
        n <- join id id -< i
        z <- abs . (-) -< (n, 100)
        case z of
          inl _ -> inr . (+) -< (n, 1)
          inr _ -> inl -< n
If you’re familiar with arrow notation, you’ll notice the above looks kinda like one big proc block. This is not a coincidence (because nothing is a coincidence). I figured if I were to go through all of this work, we might as well get a working arrow desugarer out of the mix. But I digress; that’s a story for another time.
Anyway, what’s going on here is we have an arrow count, which takes a single argument x. We then loop, starting from the value of x. Inside the loop, we now have a new variable i, which we do some voodoo on to compute n—the current value of the loop variable. Then we subtract 100 from n, and take the absolute value. The abs function here is a bit odd; it returns Left (abs x) if the input was negative, and Right x otherwise. Then we branch on the output of abs, where Left and Right have been renamed inl and inr respectively. If n - 100 was less than zero, we find ourselves in the inl case, where we add 1 to n and wrap the whole thing in inr—which the loop interprets as “loop again with this new value.” Otherwise, n - 100 was non-negative, and so we can return n directly.
Is it roundabout? You bet! The obtuseness here is not directly a feature, I was just looking for conceptually simple things I could do which would be easy to desugar into category-theoretical stuff. Which brings us to the intermediary language. After desugaring the source syntax for count above, we’re left with this IL representation:
  id △ id
⨟ cochoice
    ( undist
    ⨟   ( (prj₁ ⨟ id ▽ id) △ id
          ⨟   ( prj₁ △ 100
              ⨟ (-)
              ⨟ abs
              )
            △ id
          ⨟ prj₁ △ id
          ⨟ dist
          ⨟   ( (prj₂ ⨟ prj₂ ⨟ prj₁) △ 1
              ⨟ (+)
              ⨟ inr
              )
            ▽ ( prj₂
              ⨟ prj₂
              ⨟ prj₁
              ⨟ inl
              )
        )
      △ prj₂
    ⨟ dist
    )
⨟ prj₁
We’ll discuss all of this momentarily, but for now, just let your eyes glaze over the pretty unicode.
The underlying idea here is that each of these remaining symbols has very simple and specific algebraic semantics. For example, A ⨟ B means “do A and pipe the result into B.” By giving a transformation from this categorical IL into other domains, it becomes trivial to compile catlang to all sorts of weird compilation targets. Like SQL.
You’re probably wondering what the generated SQL looks like. Take a peek if you dare.
Ungodly Compiled SQL

f0 AS f0
FROM
(SELECT

  FROM
  (WITH t0 AS
   (SELECT *
    FROM

      clock_timestamp() as step

It’s not pretty, rather amazingly, running the above query in postgres 17 will in fact return a single row with a single column whose value is 100. And you’d better believe it does it by actually looping its way up to 100. If you don’t believe me, make the following change:
-     SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC LIMIT 1)
+     SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC)
which will instead return a row for each step of the iteration.
There are some obvious optimizations I could make to the generated SQL, but it didn’t seem worth my time, since that’s not the interesting part of the project.
What the Hell Is Going On?
Let’s take some time to discuss the underlying category theory here. I am by no means an expert, but what I have learned after a decade of bashing my head against this stuff is that a little goes a long way.
For our intents and purposes, we have types, and arrows (functions) between types. We always have the identity “do nothing arrow” id:
id  :: a ~> a
and we can compose arrows by lining up one end to another:1
(⨟) :: (a ~> b) -> (b ~> c) -> (a ~> c)
Unlike Haskell (or really any programming language, for that matter), we DO NOT have the notion of function application. That is, there is no arrow:
-- doesn't exist!
($) :: (a ~> b) -> a -> b
You can only compose arrows, you can’t apply them. That’s why we call these things “arrows” rather than “functions.”
There are a bundle of arrows for working with product types. The two projection functions correspond to fst and snd, taking individual components out of pairs:
prj₁ :: (a, b) ~> a
prj₂ :: (a, b) ~> b
How do we get things into pairs in the first place? We can use the “fork” operation, which takes two arrows computing b and c, and generates a new arrow which generates a pair of (b, c):
(△)  :: (a ~> b) -> (a ~> c) -> (a ~> (b, c))
If you’re coming from a Haskell background, it’s tempting to think of this operation merely as the (,) pair constructor. But you’ll notice from the type of the computation that there can be no data dependency between b and c, thus we are free to parallelize each side of the pair.
In category theory, the distinction between left and right sides of an arrow is rather arbitrary. This gives rise to a notion called duality where we can flip the arrows around, and get cool new behavior. If we dualize all of our product machinery, we get the coproduct machinery, where a coproduct of a and b is “either a or b, but definitely not both nor neither.”
Swapping the arrow direction of prj₁ and prj₂, and replacing (,) with Either gives us the following injections:
inl :: a ~> Either a b
inr :: b ~> Either a b
and the following “join” operation for eliminating coproducts:
(▽) :: (a ~> c) -> (b ~> c) -> (Either a b ~> c)
Again, coming from Haskell this is just the standard either function. It corresponds to a branch between one of two cases.
As you can see, with just these eight operations, we already have a tremendous amount of expressivity. We can express data dependencies via ⨟ and branching via ▽. With △ we automatically encode opportunities for parallelism, and gain the ability to build complicated data structures, with prj₁ and prj₂ allowing us to get the information back out of the data structures.
You’ll notice in the IL that there are no variable names anywhere to be found. The desugaring of the source language builds a stack (via the something to allocate △ id pattern), and replaces subsequent variable lookups with a series of projections on the stack to find the value again. On one hand, this makes the categorical IL rather hard to read, but it makes it very easy to re-target! Many domains do have a notion of grouping, but don’t have a native notion of naming.
For example, in an electronic circuit, I can have a ribbon of 32 wires which represents an Int32. If I have another ribbon of 32 wires, I can trivially route both wires into a 64-wire ribbon corresponding to a pair of (Int32, Int32).
By eliminating names before we get to the IL, it means no compiler backend ever needs to deal with names. They can just work on a stack representation, and are free to special-case optimize series of projections if they are able to.
Of particular interest to this discussion is how we desugar loops in catlang. The underlying primitive is cochoice:
cochoice :: (Either a c ~> Either b c) -> (a ~> b)
which magically turns an arrow on Eithers into an arrow without the eithers. We obviously must run that arrow on eithers. If that function returns inl, then we’re happy and we can just output that. But if the function returns inr, we have no choice but to pass it back in to the eithered arrow. In Haskell, cochoice is implemented as:
cochoiceHask :: (Either a c -> Either b c) -> a -> c
cochoiceHask f = go . Left
  where
    go :: Either a c -> b
    go eac =
      case f eac of
        Left b -> b
        Right c -> go (Right c)
which as you can see, will loop until f finally returns a Left. What’s neat about this formulation of a loop is that we can statically differentiate between our first and subsequent passes through the loop body. The first time through eac is Left, while for all other times it is Right. We don’t take advantage of it in the original count program, but how many times have you written loop code that needs to initialize something its first time through?
Compiling to SQL
So that’s the underlying theory behind the IL. How can we compile this to SQL now?
As alluded to before, we simply need to give SQL implementations for each of the operations in the intermediary language. As a simple example, id compiles to SELECT * FROM {}, where {} is the input of the arrow.
The hardest part here was working out a data representation. It seems obvious to encode each element of a product as a new column, but what do we do about coproducts? After much work thought, I decided to flatten out the coproducts. So, for example, the type:
(Int, Either Int Int)
would be represented as three columns:
( f1 INT NOT NULL
, f2 INT
, f3 INT
)
with the constraint that exactly one of f2 or f3 would be IS NOT NULL at any given point in time.
With this hammered out, almost everything else is pretty trivial. Composition corresponds to a nested query. Forks are CROSS JOINs which concatenate the columns of each sub-query. Joins are UNIONs, where we add a WHERE field IS NOT NULL clause to enforce we’re looking at the correct coproduct constructor.
Cochoice is the only really tricky thing, but it corresponds to a recursive CTE. Generating a recursive CTE table for the computation isn’t too hard, but getting the final value out of it was surprisingly tricky. The semantics of SQL tables is that they are multisets and come with an arbitrary greatest element. Which is to say, you need an column structured in a relevant way in order to query the final result. Due to some quirks in what postgres accepts, and in how I structured my queries, it was prohibitively hard to insert a “how many times have I looped” column and order by that. So instead I cheated and added a clock_timestamp() as step column which looks at the processor clock and ordered by that.
This is clearly a hack, and presumably will cause problems if I ever add some primitives which generate more than one row, but again, this is just for fun and who cares. Send me a pull request if you’re offended by my chicanery!
Stupid Directions To Go In the Future
I’ve run out of vacation time to work on this project, so I’m probably not going to get around to the meta-circular stupidity I was planning.
The compiler still needs a few string-crunching primitives (which are easy to add), but then it would be simple to write a little brainfuck interpreter in catlang. Which I could then compile to SQL. Now we’ve got a brainfuck interpreter running in postgres. Of course, this has been done by hand before, but to my knowledge, never via compilation.
There exist C to brainfuck compilers. And postgres is written in C. So in a move that would make Xzibit proud, we could run postgres in postgres. And of course, it would be fun to run brainfuck in brainfuck. That’d be a cool catlang backend if someone wanted to contribute such a thing.
Notes and Due Diligence and What Have You
I am not the first person to do anything like this. The source language of catlang is heavily inspired by Haskell’s arrow syntax, which in turn is essentially a desugaring algorithm for Arrows. Arrows are slightly the wrong abstraction because they require an operation arr :: (a -> b) -> (a ~> b)—which requires you to be able to embed Haskell functions in your category, something which is almost never possible.
Unfortunately, arrow syntax in Haskell desugars down to arr for almost everything it does, which in turn makes arrow notation effectively useless. In an ideal world, everything I described in this blog post would be a tiny little Haskell library, with arrow notation doing the heavy lifting. But that is just not the world we live in.
Nor am I the first person to notice that there are categorical semantics behind programming languages. I don’t actually know whom to cite on this one, but it is well-established folklore that the lambda calculus corresponds to cartesian-closed categories. The “closed” part of “cartesian-closed” means we have an operation eval :: (a ~> b, a) ~> b, but everyone and their dog has implemented the lambda calculus, so I thought it would be fun to see how far we can get without it. This is not a limitation on catlang’s turing completeness (since cochoice gives us everything we need.)
I’ve been thinking about writing a category-first programming language for the better part of a decade, ever since I read Compiling to Categories. That paper takes Haskell and desugars it back down to categories. I stole many of the tricks here from that paper.
Anyway. All of the code is available on github if you’re interested in taking a look. The repo isn’t up to my usual coding standards, for which you have my apologies. Of note is the template-haskell backend which can spit out Haskell code; meaning it wouldn’t be very hard to make a quasiquoter to compile catlang into what Haskell’s arrow desugaring ought to be. If there’s enough clamor for such a thing, I’ll see about turning this part into a library.
- When looking at the types of arrows in this essay, we make the distinction that ~> are arrows that we can write in catlang, while -> exist in the metatheory.↩︎

Arrows to Arrows, Categories to Queries
I’ve had a little time off of work as of late, and been spending it in characteristically unwise ways. In particular, I’ve written a little programming language that compiles to SQL. I call it catlang. That’s not to say that I’ve written a new query language. It’s a programming language, whose compiler spits out one giant SELECT statement. When you run that query in postgres, you get the output of your program.
Why have I done this? Because I needed a funny compilation target to test out the actual features of the language, which is that its intermediary language is a bunch of abstract category theory nonsense. Which I’ll get to. But I’m sure you first want to see this bad boy in action.
Behold, the function that returns 100 regardless of what input you give it. But it does it with the equivalent of a while loop:
count : Int -> Int
count =
  x ->
    loop x
      i ->
        n <- join id id -< i
        z <- abs . (-) -< (n, 100)
        case z of
          inl _ -> inr . (+) -< (n, 1)
          inr _ -> inl -< n
If you’re familiar with arrow notation, you’ll notice the above looks kinda like one big proc block. This is not a coincidence (because nothing is a coincidence). I figured if I were to go through all of this work, we might as well get a working arrow desugarer out of the mix. But I digress; that’s a story for another time.
Anyway, what’s going on here is we have an arrow count, which takes a single argument x. We then loop, starting from the value of x. Inside the loop, we now have a new variable i, which we do some voodoo on to compute n—the current value of the loop variable. Then we subtract 100 from n, and take the absolute value. The abs function here is a bit odd; it returns Left (abs x) if the input was negative, and Right x otherwise. Then we branch on the output of abs, where Left and Right have been renamed inl and inr respectively. If n - 100 was less than zero, we find ourselves in the inl case, where we add 1 to n and wrap the whole thing in inr—which the loop interprets as “loop again with this new value.” Otherwise, n - 100 was non-negative, and so we can return n directly.
Is it roundabout? You bet! The obtuseness here is not directly a feature, I was just looking for conceptually simple things I could do which would be easy to desugar into category-theoretical stuff. Which brings us to the intermediary language. After desugaring the source syntax for count above, we’re left with this IL representation:
  id △ id
⨟ cochoice
    ( undist
    ⨟   ( (prj₁ ⨟ id ▽ id) △ id
          ⨟   ( prj₁ △ 100
              ⨟ (-)
              ⨟ abs
              )
            △ id
          ⨟ prj₁ △ id
          ⨟ dist
          ⨟   ( (prj₂ ⨟ prj₂ ⨟ prj₁) △ 1
              ⨟ (+)
              ⨟ inr
              )
            ▽ ( prj₂
              ⨟ prj₂
              ⨟ prj₁
              ⨟ inl
              )
        )
      △ prj₂
    ⨟ dist
    )
⨟ prj₁
We’ll discuss all of this momentarily, but for now, just let your eyes glaze over the pretty unicode.
The underlying idea here is that each of these remaining symbols has very simple and specific algebraic semantics. For example, A ⨟ B means “do A and pipe the result into B.” By giving a transformation from this categorical IL into other domains, it becomes trivial to compile catlang to all sorts of weird compilation targets. Like SQL.
You’re probably wondering what the generated SQL looks like. Take a peek if you dare.

                  AS _)
                 SELECT *
                 FROM
                 (SELECT *
                  FROM
                  (SELECT
                   f0 AS f0
                   FROM
                   (SELECT
                    f0 AS f0
                    FROM
                    (SELECT
                     f2 AS f0, f3 AS f1, f4 AS f2, f5 AS f3
                     FROM
                     (SELECT
                      f1 AS f0, f2 AS f1, f3 AS f2, f4 AS f3, f5 AS f4, f6 AS f5
                      FROM
                      t36
                      AS _)
                     AS _)
                    AS _)
                   AS _)
                  AS _
                  CROSS JOIN
                  (SELECT f0 AS f1 FROM (SELECT 1 as f0 FROM t36 AS _) AS _))
                 AS _)
                AS _)
               AS _)
              AS _
              UNION
              SELECT *
              FROM
              (SELECT
               f0 AS f0, NULL::integer AS f1
               FROM
               (SELECT
                f0 AS f0
                FROM
                (SELECT
                 f2 AS f0, f3 AS f1, f4 AS f2, f5 AS f3
                 FROM
                 (SELECT
                  f1 AS f0, f2 AS f1, f3 AS f2, f4 AS f3, f5 AS f4, f6 AS f5
                  FROM

                   f7 AS f0, f8 AS f1, f9 AS f2, f10 AS f3, f11 AS f4, f12 AS f5, f13 AS f6
                   FROM
                   (-- join2
                    SELECT * FROM t35 AS _
                    WHERE
                    ("f7" IS NOT NULL) AND ((("f8" IS NOT NULL) OR ("f9" IS NOT NULL)) AND (("f10" IS NOT NULL) AND ((("f11" IS NOT NULL) OR ("f12" IS NOT NULL)) AND ("f13" IS NOT NULL)))))
                   AS _)
                  AS _)
                 AS _)
                AS _)
               AS _)
              AS _)
             AS _)
            AS _)
           AS _)
          AS _)
         AS _)
        AS _)
       AS _
       CROSS JOIN
       (SELECT f0 AS f2 FROM (SELECT f2 AS f0 FROM t26 AS _) AS _))
      AS _)
     SELECT *
     FROM
     (-- dist
      SELECT *
      FROM
      (SELECT
       f0 AS f0, f2 AS f1, NULL::integer AS f2, NULL::integer AS f3
       FROM
       (-- dist1
        SELECT * FROM t27 AS _ WHERE "f0" IS NOT NULL)
       AS _)
      AS _

      FROM

       NULL::integer AS f0, NULL::integer AS f1, f1 AS f2, f2 AS f3

        SELECT * FROM t27 AS _ WHERE "f1" IS NOT NULL)
       AS _)
      AS _)
     AS _)
    AS _)
   AS _)
  AS _
  WHERE
  ("f0" IS NOT NULL) AND ("f1" IS NOT NULL))
 AS _)
AS _;
It’s not pretty, rather amazingly, running the above query in postgres 17 will in fact return a single row with a single column whose value is 100. And you’d better believe it does it by actually looping its way up to 100. If you don’t believe me, make the following change:
-     SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC LIMIT 1)
+     SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC)
which will instead return a row for each step of the iteration.
There are some obvious optimizations I could make to the generated SQL, but it didn’t seem worth my time, since that’s not the interesting part of the project.
What the Hell Is Going On?
Let’s take some time to discuss the underlying category theory here. I am by no means an expert, but what I have learned after a decade of bashing my head against this stuff is that a little goes a long way.
For our intents and purposes, we have types, and arrows (functions) between types. We always have the identity “do nothing arrow” id:
id  :: a ~> a
and we can compose arrows by lining up one end to another:1
(⨟) :: (a ~> b) -> (b ~> c) -> (a ~> c)
Unlike Haskell (or really any programming language, for that matter), we DO NOT have the notion of function application. That is, there is no arrow:
-- doesn't exist!
($) :: (a ~> b) -> a -> b
You can only compose arrows, you can’t apply them. That’s why we call these things “arrows” rather than “functions.”
There are a bundle of arrows for working with product types. The two projection functions correspond to fst and snd, taking individual components out of pairs:
prj₁ :: (a, b) ~> a
prj₂ :: (a, b) ~> b
How do we get things into pairs in the first place? We can use the “fork” operation, which takes two arrows computing b and c, and generates a new arrow which generates a pair of (b, c):
(△)  :: (a ~> b) -> (a ~> c) -> (a ~> (b, c))
If you’re coming from a Haskell background, it’s tempting to think of this operation merely as the (,) pair constructor. But you’ll notice from the type of the computation that there can be no data dependency between b and c, thus we are free to parallelize each side of the pair.
In category theory, the distinction between left and right sides of an arrow is rather arbitrary. This gives rise to a notion called duality where we can flip the arrows around, and get cool new behavior. If we dualize all of our product machinery, we get the coproduct machinery, where a coproduct of a and b is “either a or b, but definitely not both nor neither.”
Swapping the arrow direction of prj₁ and prj₂, and replacing (,) with Either gives us the following injections:
inl :: a ~> Either a b
inr :: b ~> Either a b
and the following “join” operation for eliminating coproducts:
(▽) :: (a ~> c) -> (b ~> c) -> (Either a b ~> c)
Again, coming from Haskell this is just the standard either function. It corresponds to a branch between one of two cases.
As you can see, with just these eight operations, we already have a tremendous amount of expressivity. We can express data dependencies via ⨟ and branching via ▽. With △ we automatically encode opportunities for parallelism, and gain the ability to build complicated data structures, with prj₁ and prj₂ allowing us to get the information back out of the data structures.
You’ll notice in the IL that there are no variable names anywhere to be found. The desugaring of the source language builds a stack (via the something to allocate △ id pattern), and replaces subsequent variable lookups with a series of projections on the stack to find the value again. On one hand, this makes the categorical IL rather hard to read, but it makes it very easy to re-target! Many domains do have a notion of grouping, but don’t have a native notion of naming.
For example, in an electronic circuit, I can have a ribbon of 32 wires which represents an Int32. If I have another ribbon of 32 wires, I can trivially route both wires into a 64-wire ribbon corresponding to a pair of (Int32, Int32).
By eliminating names before we get to the IL, it means no compiler backend ever needs to deal with names. They can just work on a stack representation, and are free to special-case optimize series of projections if they are able to.
Of particular interest to this discussion is how we desugar loops in catlang. The underlying primitive is cochoice:
cochoice :: (Either a c ~> Either b c) -> (a ~> b)
which magically turns an arrow on Eithers into an arrow without the eithers. We obviously must run that arrow on eithers. If that function returns inl, then we’re happy and we can just output that. But if the function returns inr, we have no choice but to pass it back in to the eithered arrow. In Haskell, cochoice is implemented as:
cochoiceHask :: (Either a c -> Either b c) -> a -> c
cochoiceHask f = go . Left
  where
    go :: Either a c -> b
    go eac =
      case f eac of
        Left b -> b
        Right c -> go (Right c)
which as you can see, will loop until f finally returns a Left. What’s neat about this formulation of a loop is that we can statically differentiate between our first and subsequent passes through the loop body. The first time through eac is Left, while for all other times it is Right. We don’t take advantage of it in the original count program, but how many times have you written loop code that needs to initialize something its first time through?
Compiling to SQL
So that’s the underlying theory behind the IL. How can we compile this to SQL now?
As alluded to before, we simply need to give SQL implementations for each of the operations in the intermediary language. As a simple example, id compiles to SELECT * FROM {}, where {} is the input of the arrow.
The hardest part here was working out a data representation. It seems obvious to encode each element of a product as a new column, but what do we do about coproducts? After much work thought, I decided to flatten out the coproducts. So, for example, the type:
(Int, Either Int Int)
would be represented as three columns:
( f1 INT NOT NULL
, f2 INT
, f3 INT
)
with the constraint that exactly one of f2 or f3 would be IS NOT NULL at any given point in time.
With this hammered out, almost everything else is pretty trivial. Composition corresponds to a nested query. Forks are CROSS JOINs which concatenate the columns of each sub-query. Joins are UNIONs, where we add a WHERE field IS NOT NULL clause to enforce we’re looking at the correct coproduct constructor.
Cochoice is the only really tricky thing, but it corresponds to a recursive CTE. Generating a recursive CTE table for the computation isn’t too hard, but getting the final value out of it was surprisingly tricky. The semantics of SQL tables is that they are multisets and come with an arbitrary greatest element. Which is to say, you need an column structured in a relevant way in order to query the final result. Due to some quirks in what postgres accepts, and in how I structured my queries, it was prohibitively hard to insert a “how many times have I looped” column and order by that. So instead I cheated and added a clock_timestamp() as step column which looks at the processor clock and ordered by that.
This is clearly a hack, and presumably will cause problems if I ever add some primitives which generate more than one row, but again, this is just for fun and who cares. Send me a pull request if you’re offended by my chicanery!
Stupid Directions To Go In the Future
I’ve run out of vacation time to work on this project, so I’m probably not going to get around to the meta-circular stupidity I was planning.
The compiler still needs a few string-crunching primitives (which are easy to add), but then it would be simple to write a little brainfuck interpreter in catlang. Which I could then compile to SQL. Now we’ve got a brainfuck interpreter running in postgres. Of course, this has been done by hand before, but to my knowledge, never via compilation.
There exist C to brainfuck compilers. And postgres is written in C. So in a move that would make Xzibit proud, we could run postgres in postgres. And of course, it would be fun to run brainfuck in brainfuck. That’d be a cool catlang backend if someone wanted to contribute such a thing.
Notes and Due Diligence and What Have You
I am not the first person to do anything like this. The source language of catlang is heavily inspired by Haskell’s arrow syntax, which in turn is essentially a desugaring algorithm for Arrows. Arrows are slightly the wrong abstraction because they require an operation arr :: (a -> b) -> (a ~> b)—which requires you to be able to embed Haskell functions in your category, something which is almost never possible.
Unfortunately, arrow syntax in Haskell desugars down to arr for almost everything it does, which in turn makes arrow notation effectively useless. In an ideal world, everything I described in this blog post would be a tiny little Haskell library, with arrow notation doing the heavy lifting. But that is just not the world we live in.
Nor am I the first person to notice that there are categorical semantics behind programming languages. I don’t actually know whom to cite on this one, but it is well-established folklore that the lambda calculus corresponds to cartesian-closed categories. The “closed” part of “cartesian-closed” means we have an operation eval :: (a ~> b, a) ~> b, but everyone and their dog has implemented the lambda calculus, so I thought it would be fun to see how far we can get without it. This is not a limitation on catlang’s turing completeness (since cochoice gives us everything we need.)
I’ve been thinking about writing a category-first programming language for the better part of a decade, ever since I read Compiling to Categories. That paper takes Haskell and desugars it back down to categories. I stole many of the tricks here from that paper.
Anyway. All of the code is available on github if you’re interested in taking a look. The repo isn’t up to my usual coding standards, for which you have my apologies. Of note is the template-haskell backend which can spit out Haskell code; meaning it wouldn’t be very hard to make a quasiquoter to compile catlang into what Haskell’s arrow desugaring ought to be. If there’s enough clamor for such a thing, I’ll see about turning this part into a library.
- When looking at the types of arrows in this essay, we make the distinction that ~> are arrows that we can write in catlang, while -> exist in the metatheory.↩︎

1 comment
When you send a POST request to your server, you think you're sending the information to YOUR server, right? That was the default behaviour - as it should be. After updating the Postman client, I noticed Postman also sends the request to their internal servers, which then sends your server the actual request (proxying). I thought I was paranoid until another commenter confirmed the same (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50358055). It's fucking annoying that something called POSTman does anything but that. Please don't use Postman for anything sensitive. It's borderline spyware, especially when you didn't consent to this behavior.

AMD rides data center riches to &#8216;largest and most profitable&#8217; quarter in history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
01:17:17 UTC

AMD CEO Lisa Su said in the company’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday that Q3 2026 was “was the largest and most profitable in our history.” AMD reported a record $13.4 billion in quarterly revenue, and it’s predicting it will hit another record high next quarter of $17 billion. The company’s data center business is driving that growth, with $8.5 billion in data center quarterly revenue for Q3 2026. Su said AMD’s expecting its revenue to “grow more than 80 percent in 2027,” adding that “data center will be the largest contributor.”
AMD rides data center riches to ‘largest and most profitable’ quarter in history
AMD thinks over 80 percent of its revenue will eventually come from its data center business alone.
Eventually, most of AMD’s revenue might come from its data center business. In response to a question during Tuesday’s earnings call, CFO Jean Hu said, “Looking ahead of 2027, we actually think our data center business will be more than 80 percent of total company revenue.”
As of Q3 2026, roughly 63 percent of AMD’s net quarterly revenue was from its data center business. Over the last couple years, jumps in the company’s revenue have been closely mirroring its data center business — in Q3 2026 its overall revenue went up $1.9 billion, while its data center revenue went up $1.8 billion.
As AMD keeps smashing its data center revenue records, its gaming business dropped 40 percent compared to last year, dipping to $773 million. PCs, game consoles, and other tech have been hit with price hikes over recent months due to shortages of RAM and other components, driven by demand from AI data centers. The shortage might not end anytime soon — Intel said it’s not expecting the shortage to improve next year, and SK Hynix predicted it’ll last until 2030.
Su acknowledged the price hikes, saying, “Our view is, this is one of those times — when, you know, component prices go up, it affects overall system pricing. One would expect the consumer markets to be more sensitive to that, and so we have seen a bit of a slowdown in the sell-through.” Su added, “We are planning with the current environment for a down year for 2027.”

The biggest modding site in PC gaming is taking a stance on AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
00:42:54 UTC
09:42:54 KST

The PC gaming mods repository Nexus Mods is making disclosures about AI mandatory for uploads of new mods, meaning that mod authors will have to declare “whether AI has been used in their work,” the site announced today as part of a big post about AI-generated content on the platform.
The biggest modding site in PC gaming is taking a stance on AI
Nexus Mods says that authors of newly uploaded mods will have to declare whether AI was ‘used in their work.’
“One of the most consistent concerns we’ve heard is that it’s not clearly disclosed when AI has been used to create a mod,” according to the post from site owner Victor “Foledinho” Folmann. “We already have tags for AI-generated and AI-assisted mods, but we recognise that there’s a lot more we can do to make that information more accessible and clear for you all.” Any mods tagged as “AI-assisted” will also be required to include “a public explanation of how and where AI was used.” AI tags will also be “more prominent” on mod pages.
Folmann says Nexus Mods is “pro-human creativity” but “won’t introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods.” As for why that is:
The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We’d prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.
Folmann notes that Nexus Mods won’t use mods to train AI and “will not sell or license them to anyone doing so.” However, the site is working on “clearer control” over how mods can be reused on others and strengthening attribution for when “a mod uses another Mod Author’s mod with the appropriate permissions.”
Nexus Mods is also making changes to the Recently Added section of the site to address a problem of mod authors uploading many mods at once, which makes other mods fall down down the page. “This is less of an issue related to AI, but it’s becoming much more prevalent as mod production is speeding up,” Folmann says. The changes include trying limits on how many mods from one author are shown at a time and “tighter restrictions” on uploads from new accounts. The platform is also launching controls to hide AI-generated content in game pages and on the homepage, and “next up,” in search.
Nexus Mods’ full AI policy is here, and mod authors have 60 days to update their existing mods to meet the requirements. The 60-day grace period ends on January 2nd, and after that time, the site will begin enforcing the rules.

C++26 Disapproved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
00:33:22 UTC
09:33:22 KST

C++26 DIS failed, how does C++ survive?
On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved!
I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views.
The Current Status
As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote.
In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures, there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved.
The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release.
The Process
Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree.
However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently.
The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026.
It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me.
The History of Contracts in C++
The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote.
In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes.
And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached.
What happens next?
The big problem: what happens next? ISO, of course, has a process for this. It offers various options:
- Submit a revised draft for a new DIS vote.
- Submit a revised draft to the committee (that would be the CD phase).
- Publish a revised draft as a Technical Specification.
- Cancel the project.
All of these possibilities mean a delay in the next C++ standard. Whether it will still be called C++26 is also up in the air, but that’s a much smaller issue.
The difficulty with all four options is that they require a majority within WG21. However, this working group voted to move C++26 with Contracts into the next voting phase leading to its release. And it did so with more than just the required two-thirds majority. The feature didn’t come out of nowhere, either; it was developed over the course of years through the work and possibly personal commitment of many people. It’s hard to imagine that this group would simply want to abandon its work, which has received approval on multiple occasions so far. The same applies to the group that is dissatisfied with Contracts. This group, too, has invested effort, in some cases even in alternative implementations. It’s hard to imagine that, after these groups voted “no” in the DIS vote, the result would change without Contracts being removed.
Even the last option removing C++26 requires a majority in WG21. As I understand it, this step would mean reverting to C++23 and proceeding to C++29 without a single change. This would affect the work of even more people. WG21 would then be tasked with incorporating features that have already been successfully included in C++26 into C++29. Since this can only be done through a paper backed by at least one person advocating for it, features could be omitted if that person lacks the motivation or time.
Of course, certainty about the voting outcome can only be achieved if the respective path is actually taken.
Unfortunately, the way forward is currently more than uncertain. Perhaps this also explains why ISO/IEC DIS 26926 marked the end of this activity. Consensus is needed to move forward. Trust is always required for consensus. Unfortunately, that trust has just been shaken.
The next C++ standard, and thus the future of C++, is currently at an impasse.
The good news is that the next meeting will take place on November 16, which is just a few days away. The top priority will be to break the deadlock. This will very likely have implications for C++29 as well; in fact, there is currently no reason to continue working on this project.
My Personal Opinion
Normally, my articles are technically focused and free of personal opinion. Regarding the rejected DIS, I can only say that I consider it a massive disaster and feel sorry for the entire C++ community. Regardless of whether someone likes Contracts, considers them important, or sees major weaknesses in them, the topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting “no,” an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken. Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes. Overall, the result is one in which all participants have given their best. During the DIS vote, the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust.
Andreas

C++26 Disapproved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
00:33:22 UTC
09:33:22 KST

C++26 DIS failed, how does C++ survive?
On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved!
I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views.
The Current Status
As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote.
In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures, there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved.
The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release.
The Process
Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree.
However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently.
The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026.
It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me.
The History of Contracts in C++
The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote.
In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes.
And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached.
What happens next?
The big problem: what happens next? ISO, of course, has a process for this. It offers various options:
- Submit a revised draft for a new DIS vote.
- Submit a revised draft to the committee (that would be the CD phase).
- Publish a revised draft as a Technical Specification.
- Cancel the project.
All of these possibilities mean a delay in the next C++ standard. Whether it will still be called C++26 is also up in the air, but that’s a much smaller issue.
The difficulty with all four options is that they require a majority within WG21. However, this working group voted to move C++26 with Contracts into the next voting phase leading to its release. And it did so with more than just the required two-thirds majority. The feature didn’t come out of nowhere, either; it was developed over the course of years through the work and possibly personal commitment of many people. It’s hard to imagine that this group would simply want to abandon its work, which has received approval on multiple occasions so far. The same applies to the group that is dissatisfied with Contracts. This group, too, has invested effort, in some cases even in alternative implementations. It’s hard to imagine that, after these groups voted “no” in the DIS vote, the result would change without Contracts being removed.

This would affect the work of even more people. WG21 would then be tasked with incorporating features that have already been successfully included in C++26 into C++29. Since this can only be done through a paper backed by at least one person advocating for it, features could be omitted if that person lacks the motivation or time.

Unfortunately, the way forward is currently more than uncertain. Perhaps this also explains why ISO/IEC DIS 26926 marked the end of this activity. Consensus is needed to move forward. Trust is always required for consensus. Unfortunately, that trust has just been shaken.

Developers can also add a tag that causes Safari to ignore Adaptive Dark Mode and show the website as the developer intended.

Prompting Is Programming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
23:49:06 UTC
08:49:06 KST

Prompting Is Programming
The other day I watched a friend of mine, an Ivy League-educated professor in the liberal arts, work with Claude. The conversation went in circles, and they never articulated what their goal was. Each reply from Claude was reasonable given what it had been told, and each one was a little off from what my friend actually wanted, so they’d nudge it, and it would drift somewhere else. This is one of the smartest people I know, and I was watching them struggle with a tool that has completely reshaped the way I build software.
That interaction came to mind when I was reading about how industries outside of software aren’t seeing productivity gains from AI. Marketers, analysts, managers, and operations folks get some help drafting emails and summarizing meetings, then spend the time they saved cleaning up plausible-looking output that doesn’t quite do what they needed. The org-wide productivity gains that were promised mostly haven’t materialized. For software engineers, the change is night and day. I basically stopped writing code within a few weeks of Opus 4.5 shipping, and nearly every engineer I know has a version of that story.
The usual explanations are that the models were trained on mountains of code, that code is verifiable because it either compiles and passes the tests or it doesn’t, and that the AI labs poured their best tooling effort into coding agents because their own employees are engineers. All of that is true. None of it fully explains the gap, because I’ve watched other engineers, and experienced it myself, get great results out of these tools on tasks that have nothing to do with code, like planning a trip, restructuring a budget, or drafting a grant proposal.
My theory is simpler. Prompting an AI well is programming. The mental work is the same; only the syntax changed. Engineers are good at it because they’ve spent years doing it, and most other people haven’t done it at all.
Consider what goes through your mind when you write a function or class. You decide what the inputs are and where they come from. You decide exactly what the output should look like. You break the problem into steps small enough that each one is obviously right. You think about the edge cases: the empty list, the missing field, the user who does something you didn’t expect. You decide how you’ll know it works. None of that is about typing semicolons, and all of it is what separates a good prompt from a bad one. A starting state and a goal state are the first things a programmer writes down, even if only in their head. They were exactly what was missing from my friend’s session.
A non-programmer asks the agent to “put together a report on Q3 sales.” An engineer, without really thinking about it, asks a different question: which data, in which file, broken down by what, compared against what baseline, in what format, and what should happen with the two regions that reorganized mid-quarter? The engineer isn’t smarter. My friend could run circles around most engineers I know intellectually. The engineer has just had the precision beaten into them by a compiler.
Every programmer spent years being told, instantly and without mercy, that the computer does what you said rather than what you meant. Non-programmers have spent their careers communicating with humans, who fill in the gaps with shared context and common sense, and who come back with a clarifying question when they’re confused. An LLM also fills in the gaps, but it fills them with the most plausible guess and rarely asks. A vague prompt doesn’t throw an error. The model hallucinates what you meant, hands back something that looks about right, and leaves you to discover where it isn’t. An engineer’s instinct is to distrust output that looks about right. Most people’s instinct is to accept it.
The gap gets wider when the output is wrong. An engineer debugs. They form a hypothesis about which part of their instructions led the model astray, change that one thing, and run it again. A non-programmer tends to reroll the same prompt, append “please be accurate,” or conclude that the tool doesn’t work. They’ve never had to build the habit of treating a bad result as information about their own input.
This complicates something I wrote in May. I argued that domain expertise is the real moat, and that a domain expert with an agent can be startlingly effective because they know what right looks like. I still believe the oracle matters. But knowing what right looks like is a judging skill, and it only kicks in once the agent has produced something worth judging. Getting it there is a specifying skill, and that one is computational. When I look at the non-engineers who really are getting enormous value from these tools, they almost always have a programmer’s brain hiding under a different job title: the finance person who builds elaborate spreadsheets with lookup tables, the ops manager who writes their own Zapier flows, the researcher who wrangles data in R because nobody else would. They were programming all along. They just didn’t call it that.
Which brings me back to my friend. They didn’t need a better prompt template or a list of magic phrases. They needed the habits any second-year computer science student has without thinking about them: say what done looks like before you start, break the work into pieces small enough to check, and when the answer comes back wrong, ask what in your own instructions sent it there. None of that requires knowing a programming language. It does require years of being corrected by a compiler, and most brilliant people have never spent a single afternoon on the receiving end of one.
Natural language programming was sold as a way to let everyone program. So far it mostly lets people who already think like programmers do it faster, in English.

People, including on this staff, keep asking me with varying degrees of excitement or trepidation when the AI bubble will burst. Maybe run a cat sanctuary, who knows.
Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!
I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!
What I can tell you is that I read with interest a story in Bloomberg this morning: “Wall Street CEOs, Big Money Managers Divided Over AI Risks.” The story itself is a roundup of stuff said at the 2026 Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. Here’s what caught my attention: The CEO of Pacific Investment Management Co. — that’s PIMCO, the legendary bond firm — told listeners that there’s going to be a downturn in the AI market “and then things are going to break.”
“What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
The astronomically expensive AI buildout has swamped debt markets — making it harder to raise cash. But there’s still more debt coming, and people still want to buy it. Even Microsoft recently sold bonds, for the first time in a decade — $25 billion of them.
The PIMCO CEO — his name is Emmanuel Roman, but his job is what matters here — has estimated that the AI buildout could create $2 trillion in financing needs over the next five years. The entire total US bond market is about $12 trillion.
I am harping on PIMCO because it has been instrumental in the AI trade. It was among the group of financiers that did the first CoreWeave chip-based financing in 2023. It made a quick $2 billion in paper gains from $29 billion in Meta bonds, meant to support the AI buildout, last year. It bought $4 billion of SpaceX bonds last month. If PIMCO’s CEO is publicly sounding the alarm about a bubble popping, that’s a big deal — especially since the company just sold a bunch of its AI debt.
It’s not just PIMCO urging caution. Apollo Global Management, which lately had been talking with SpaceX about a $40 billion chip deal, is also warning of AI risk. Apollo president Jim Zelter told analysts today that while he expects society will use “dramatically more computing power in the future” and that AI is improving quickly, there is still significant uncertainty. “What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
The sheer volume of interest on Meta’s bonds suggests we are not at the top of the market. But there have been reports from China that its AI bubble burst some time ago. Meanwhile Wall Street banks were tripping over themselves to finance $63 billion in debt from Anthropic — not even a hyperscaler.
This is what I mean when I say “I don’t know.” I do think, though, that something major — PIMCO’s Roman singled out US rate hikes, war, or a eurozone crisis as potential triggers — could flip this market. We’re not in go-go-go territory now. Maybe that will change; it’s possible Anthropic’s IPO will go blockbuster and it’ll be like when someone rolls up to a party that’s running low on beer with a 24-pack. But as more people are expressing caution — and particularly after the disaster at Situational Awareness — the best part of the party might be over.

EU Court Advisor Warns Google AI Chatbot May Breach Copyright Rules

EU Court Advisor Warns Google AI Chatbot May Breach Copyright Rules 19
			
		 	
				An adviser to the EU's highest court says Google's Gemini may violate publishers' copyright when it reproduces recognizable portions of their articles or circumvents paywalls and other technical protections to generate answers. Reuters reports:  The case before the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice of the European Union pitted Hungarian website operator Like Company against US-based Google's artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. A ruling against Google, which could force the tech giant to pay fees for the use of such content, could throw a lifeline to online media such as Like Company. They have seen traffic dwindle as news summaries written by AI chatbots like Gemini increasingly replace traditional search engines' results, which include hyperlinks to the media websites.
"When an LLM (large language model)-driven chatbot retrieves a publication from a press publisher's website, reuses that publication to generate an answer, and provides that answer to the user, the press publisher's right may be infringed in certain circumstances," Advocate General Maciej Szpunar said. Gemini's answers fall under the publishers' right of reproduction when chatbots access publications by unlawfully "circumventing paywalls or other technical barriers, or when they reuse "the form of expression of that publication in a recognizable manner," he said.
Copyright rules do not protect the "mere facts" reported by press publications, but "only the specific form of expression," he added. On the other hand, he said, the use of material protected by copyright to train LLMs -- AI systems that use vast amounts of text to generate human-like responses and summarize information -- is "freely permitted under the text and data mining exception." Szpunar said there was no evidence that Google had used the Hungarian publisher's articles to train Gemini. The court, which follows the majority of its advisers' non-binding opinions, will rule in the coming months.  "Google's powerful gatekeeping role in search makes this particularly important. Publishers depend on Google to reach readers, while Google increasingly delivers AI-generated answers directly to users," said Angela Mills Wade, the council's executive director.
"Publishers should not have to choose between search visibility and protecting their rights. Nor should Google's control over access to audiences become leverage to secure publishers' content for AI services," she said.

Search queries are growing at their fastest rate in five years, Google parent Alphabet said in its earnings report last week. However, Google’s Search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent year over year in the third quarter, down from roughly 17 percent in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, growth in paid clicks — clicks on ads that generate revenue for Google — slowed from 13 percent to 8 percent.
Google hasn’t figured out how to make AI pay like its search engine
Google says AI is boosting searches, but that activity isn’t translating into faster growth for the business that pays for it.
That’s still substantial growth, but not the direction investors were hoping for from a company planning to spend about $200 billion this year on infrastructure, largely to support AI. Alphabet shares have fallen about 14 percent since it reported earnings last week, as investors question the costs and returns of the company’s AI ambitions.
“This is the first major disruption that Google is facing to its core business in decades.”
Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said currency effects were the biggest driver of the revenue-growth slowdown, alongside changes in spending by advertisers in particular industries. But Google’s AI makeover also contributed to the slowdown: AI Mode queries were growing strongly but monetizing at a lower rate than traditional searches, Schindler says. He added that Google feels good about its trajectory and that its “ad experiments have shown promising results.”
It remains unclear whether that reflects a deliberate rollout of ads, as Google says, or a more fundamental problem with advertising in AI search.
YOY growth for search revenue vs. paid clicks in Q1-3 in 2026
“This is the first major disruption that Google is facing to its core business in decades,” Nate Elliott, an eMarketer principal analyst covering AI and advertising, tells The Verge. AI is changing how people find information — and whether they click on the ads that fund Google’s business.
What Google’s core Search business looks like increasingly depends on what you ask. In many cases, AI Overviews add generated summaries to search results; electing AI Mode turns searching into a conversation. But someone searching for Nikes can still get familiar shopping listings and text ads, says Andy Taylor, vice president of research at digital advertising agency Tinuiti. They’re looking to buy shoes rather than get an AI explanation of them.
Google’s argument is that AI is expanding the business. Schindler says most AI Mode queries are “incremental” — additional questions rather than replacements for existing searches. Many are also “upper-funnel,” meaning people are researching potential purchases before they know what they want. The company sees those searches as opportunities to sell more ads over time.
Google is currently expanding ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode, including internationally and across multiple turns of US AI Mode conversations. It has also floated bringing ads to its standalone Gemini app, saying formats developed for AI Mode could carry over, but hasn’t announced when.
The thing is, Google, as well as competitors like OpenAI, are still figuring out how to make ads work in AI — both delivering results for advertisers and avoiding alienating the people using their AI tools.
For now, advertisers are still getting results from Google. Tinuiti’s same-store advertisers increased their Google paid search spending 14 percent year over year in the third quarter while maintaining their return-on-ad-spend targets.
“If people are clicking through less often. That is a challenge that they need to figure out.”
“We’re still seeing a good return, and we’re not seeing performance take a hit,” Taylor says.
The catch is that advertisers can’t isolate how Google’s AI ads are doing. Google doesn’t let them separately target that inventory or break out its performance, Taylor says. Steady overall returns could mean AI ad traffic is still too small to noticeably affect the results, or that it performs similarly to existing inventory. Taylor suspects it’s mostly the former.
That leaves an important question unanswered: How much will AI add to Google’s advertising business, and how much could it replace? Additional queries could bring in new revenue even if each earns less than a traditional search. The risk is that AI Mode also draws people away from searches that Google monetizes more effectively. Google’s claim that most AI Mode queries are additional doesn’t tell us how much revenue it could lose from the searches AI Mode replaces.
“If people are clicking through less often,” Elliott says, “that is a challenge that they need to figure out.”
The promise of conversational advertising is that people share much more about their needs than they would in a few keywords. But platforms still have to identify which parts of a conversation matter and match them with the right ads.
“It’s not a slam dunk that it’s going to turn into more effective advertising,” Elliott says.
An early study of ChatGPT ads suggests richer conversations don’t automatically translate into more retail sales. An October working paper found that US visits from ChatGPT ads generated 64 percent less revenue for retailers per session than visits from Google Search ads: $0.89 versus $2.45. The working paper measures retailers’ sales rather than platform revenue, and its findings about ChatGPT don’t establish how Google’s own AI ads perform.
Taylor cautions that those comparisons depend on what people are searching for. Someone searching Google for Nike shoes may already be ready to buy, while someone asking an AI tool which running shoes to choose is still researching. A higher sales return could reflect that difference in purchase intent rather than more effective ads.
Google’s existing business has given it room to take its time with AI ads, Taylor says. He points to its successful shift to mobile: Early phone traffic was less valuable to advertisers because shopping on a phone was cumbersome, but that changed.
Elliott cautions that finding effective ad formats can take years. Search engines started with banner ads before adopting paid listings; social media went through its own experimentation. Today’s formats may not be the ones that ultimately work.
But Google’s mounting AI spending raises the stakes. Search revenue is still growing by double digits, but the company has yet to show how well its new way of searching can pay.
“They absolutely do not have it all figured out,” Elliott says. “No one has it all figured out.”
